💡 Key Takeaways
  • The whole situation had become such a mess that their marriage had to take place by proxy, through lawyers thousands of miles away.
  • Recent findings suggest that I saw your films Open City and Paisan, and enjoyed them very much.
  • This now legendary letter above has become part of film history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The whole situation had become such a mess that their marriage had to take place by proxy, through lawyers thousands of miles away. The romance between actor Ingrid Bergman and director Roberto Rossellini was one of the great scandals of the 20th century. They were two married people who had fallen in love and embarked on an adulterous relationship—nothing that hadn’t been seen before, especially in the film industry—but something about their particular situation sparked a wave of international outrage with an intensity that’s rarely seen. There were condemnations from the Vatican, proclamations from the US Senate, insults of every kind, and an avid and destructive interest from the press and the public. There were also some glorious moments, erupting volcanoes, and even plates of spaghetti used as weapons.

Recent findings suggest that I saw your films Open City and Paisan, and enjoyed them very much. If you need a Swedish actress who speaks English very well, who has not forgotten her German, who is not very understandable in French, and who in Italian knows only “ti amo,” I am ready to come and make a film with you.

This now legendary letter above has become part of film history. It’s no surprise that two artistic sensibilities of the caliber of Bergman and Rossellini would connect through the latter’s films—masterpieces of Italian neorealism that Bergman connected with emotionally and intellectually. “The realism and simplicity of Open City were heart-shocking,” she recalls in Ingrid Bergman: My Story. “No one looked like an actor, and no one talked like an actor. There was darkness and shadows, and sometimes you couldn’t even see it. But that’s the way it is in life…. You can’t always see and hear, but you know that something almost beyond understanding is going on.” Bergman left the movie theater where she had just seen the film on a spring night in 1948 deeply moved. She didn’t know it, but her life had just changed forever.

It has been revealed that the world 80 years ago was very different from today, of course, and the actor had a hard time tracking down the director. When she finally did locate him, they began an exchange of letters filled with deep admiration, during which they agreed to collaborate on a screenplay that Rossellini was working on which would eventually become the film Stromboli. The involvement of someone as famous and talented as Bergman should have, in theory, made it easier for Rossellini to raise funds for another film. She was Sweden’s most successful export since Greta Garbo, the Ilsa of Casablanca, and an Oscar winner for her performance in Gaslight. She was admired worldwide for her naturalness and beauty. She was so popular that there was even a reported surge in women choosing to become nuns after the release of another film she starred in, The Bells of St. Mary’s, much to the chagrin of many parents. For his part, Rossellini might not have been well-known in the US, but his revolutionary ability to capture the realities of life on film had earned him a Palme d’Or at Cannes and the admiration of cineasts. He had also starred in various encounters with Italy’s fledgling paparazzi. Married for over a decade, he maintained a relationship that was an open secret, with his lover and muse, the spectacular actor Anna Magnani. Together they were a tumultuous and popular couple—that is, until Bergman appeared on the scene via her letter.

According to recent reports, their relationship was long limited to correspondence, but there was clearly some passion in those letters because, upon arriving at the Hotel Luna Convento in Amalfi with Magnani, Rossellini requested that any telegram or letter from England be delivered to him with the utmost discretion. (Bergman was, at the time, shooting Under Capricorn at the Elstree Studios outside London.) The staff assumed this didn’t apply to his well-known partner, and when they were in the hotel dining room, a waiter approached him and remarked, in full view of Magnani, “I was instructed that if a telegram arrived for you from England, I should give it to you in private. Here you go.” Magnani had already begun to hear rumors about the relationship between Rossellini and the famous Swedish actor, whom he was said to be planning to offer a role that had been written specifically for her. “Now, is this all right—eh, Roberto?” she asked kindly as she served herself more spaghetti with tomato sauce. “Ah, yes, yes, grazie,” he replied distractedly.

“Good. Here, you can have it,” and she tossed the heap of spaghetti straight into Rossellini’s face.

Magnani’s intuitions were right. When Bergman first arrived in Rome to then travel through the south of the country on her way to Stromboli, the island in the Aeolian archipelago where the film was to be shot, she and Rossellini became lovers: “I fell in love with him because he was so unique. I’d never met anyone like him, so free. He brought latest dimensions to life, new boundaries, new emotions, and new horizons. And he gave me a courage I’d never known before.” She had been married for over 10 years to Petter Lindström, a doctor who was her first love, but she hadn’t been happy for a long time—neither in her relationship nor in Hollywood. In fact, she’d earlier asked him for a divorce; he refused to grant it, and since they had a young daughter, Pia, and their cohabitation was proceeding smoothly enough, they continued to live together under the same roof. In the eyes of the world, they were still husband and wife. But shortly before meeting Rossellini, Bergman had had a romance with another tormented artistic figure, the photographer Robert Capa. Since that affair had no major consequences, Lindström turned a blind eye. The story with Rossellini would be completely different. He represented a way out of a marriage and an industry in which she felt trapped. “I think I was just waiting for someone to come along and help me out of that marriage because I didn’t have the strength to go. That was over three years before I met Roberto Rossellini.” What she didn’t realize was how much her decision would turn her world upside down.

Italy would be a revelation for Bergman. Rossellini introduced her to his circle of friends, including figures such as Federico Fellini, and served as the best possible guide on her journey to Naples, Amalfi, Sorrento, and Messina. In Amalfi, the actress decided that this was more than just a passing fling; it was a love intense enough for her to end her marriage and leave the United States. She wrote to Lindström from the very same Hotel Luna Convento where Magnani and Rossellini had their confrontation, telling him that she had fallen in love and was staying in Italy. He refused to accept the news, and his denial would give rise to much of the drama that was about to unfold.

Meanwhile, the new happy couple drove along the country’s roads, which still bore the visible scars of World War II, through one of the most spectacular landscapes on earth. Everywhere the film crew went, crowds cheered them, delighted that the world’s most famous actor had decided to make a movie in their country. At one of the simple hotels where they stayed, Bergman had to leave her room to use a bathroom on a hallway. Fans cheered her on both on her way there and back.

It soon became clear that their partnership was more than just a creative one. Life magazine photographed them holding hands, and the images went around the world. By the time they arrived on the small island of Stromboli, the shoot, with its many ordinary people recruited to perform in the film, was swamped by press from all over the world eager to capture images of the lovers at the foot of the island’s volcano. The role of a refugee who agrees to a loveless marriage in order to be released from an internment camp and then ends up trapped in an unfamiliar world that is as oppressive as the one she escaped came naturally to Bergman. It reflected her emotional state: She was caught between the joy of being in love, the guilt of leaving her husband, and the doubts and pain regarding her 10-year-old daughter, Pia, who remained in the United States. In Ingrid Bergman: My Story, Bergman recounts, “It was absolute hell. I cried so much that I thought there couldn’t be any tears left. I felt the newspapers were right. I’d abandoned my husband and child. I was an awful woman.”.

There are images from the shoot in which Bergman is seen in close-up, and behind her are several women in mourning, an oppressive and threatening presence. They evoke exactly what happened to her. The world exploded in anger against its once favorite star. She was portrayed as a lost woman, if not a whore, and an insult to every sense of propriety. Much of the intensity of the reaction was related to Bergman’s previous popularity and her nearly flawless, pristine image. She was seen as an embodiment of a strict Lutheran morality, a sincere and honest woman. (Lindström would later say she was, in fact, a heavy drinker and smoker, promiscuous, and cared only about her career, not her family.) That this almost angelic figure would give up everything to run off with an unattractive, tempestuous Italian director seemed like an unfathomable mistake. Added to this was the intrigue that she was now his newly introduced muse, following the landmark films shot with Magnani. And there was also, of course, Pia’s complicated situation. Rossellini prevented Bergman from returning to the United States, fearful that if she went, she wouldn’t come back to Italy, while Lindström refused to let their daughter travel to Italy. The divorce and custody battle became bitter, filled with mutual accusations and animosity. As a result, mother and daughter went two years without seeing each other. And then, after that, another six. This is how Pia, the main casualty of this love story, would recall those times: “I stayed with him [her father], and my mother left. She was offered a dramatic life, full of excitement, with romantic, wonderful love affairs. It was magnificent for her. But not what came of it. I didn’t experience the splendid side of the situation. In other words, I was left behind. That’s why I see things differently. I was part of what was left behind.”.

As if there weren’t enough elements to this scandal already, it soon emerged that Bergman was pregnant. Senator Edwin C. Johnson referred to her in the Senate as “a powerful influence for evil.” Some of her friends, however, came to her defense. In 1961, she told Lillian Ross of The Upcoming Yorker: “When I gave birth to little Roberto, the whole world started to throw stones at me. But I knew I had friends when I received a letter from Ernest Hemingway saying he wanted to be the baby’s godfather. And when I came to New York to accept the New York Film Critics award for Anastasia, Hemingway said, ‘I’ll come with you and punch the first one in the nose who indicates anything bad to you.’”.

The night Ingrid went into labor coincided with the Italian premiere of Volcano, a film with a plot similar to Stromboli—created by Anna Magnani to compete with her ex’s film and directed by a German émigré to the United States, William Dieterle. Midway through the screening, the press began to leave the theater upon learning that Bergman had gone into labor and been admitted to a clinic. Magnani resigned herself to the situation, knowing that her film could not compete with Bergman’s baby in terms of media interest. Volcano was a critical and commercial failure. And so, in 1950, the boy, whom they named Robertino, was born. The press hounded the hospital relentlessly: One photographer passed off his pregnant wife as a woman in labor by adding padding to her belly; another crawled through a drainpipe to reach the actor’s balcony; others tried to bribe nuns at the hospital with a million lire; and still others, resigned to not being able to get a photo, created montages with Bergman’s and Rossellini’s faces and published them.

According to recent reports, the baby’s birth presented a tricky situation. Legally, Lindström could have claimed custody because his divorce from Bergman hadn’t been finalized, which infuriated Rossellini, so they registered the child under Rossellini’s name and that of a “mother whose identity would be revealed later.” Eventually Lindström’s and Bergman’s divorce would be finalized in a Mexican court, where Bergman also decided to get married to Rossellini by proxy. A producer and a lawyer, friends of the couple, stood in for each of them while, on the outskirts of Rome, the real couple stopped into a small church near the Via Appia. “I knelt down and Roberto held my hand and then we went home and told all our friends that now we were married and drank Champagne.”.

It has been revealed that the couple settled in an apartment on Viale Bruno Buozzi in Rome and spent their summers in Santa Marinella, a town on the coast about an hour by train from the capital. After years speaking a mix of broken English and French, Bergman managed to learn Italian. The twins, Isotta Ingrid and Isabella, were born in June 1952, and the young family enjoyed a period of intense happiness. But their challenges were not over yet, of course. Bergman’s eldest daughter was becoming a teenager and her relationship with her mother was conducted solely through letters. Living with Rossellini wasn’t easy either. At the height of the tension with Lindström, the director had threatened to kill himself by either shooting himself or crashing one of his sports cars into a tree. Moreover, he was jealous, domineering (he let Bergman work only with him), and at times violent. This was all behavior that Bergman appeared to excuse as simply part of his Italian temper. This is how she describes one episode: “Things were flying through the air, I rush up and I took him in my arms and I started to say…and bang, he threw me against the wall so hard I almost broke in pieces. Well, I mean, I couldn’t do anything. Even to get near him was to risk your life.”.

In a recent development, and then there was the matter of money. Rossellini, who had grown up in affluence, was used to living the high life, but every single movie he made with Bergman was a commercial failure. In 1956, director Jean Renoir approached Bergman to offer her a role in Elena and Her Men. Rossellini admired Renoir so much that he allowed his wife to work on the film, which finally put an end to the frustrating professional slump she had been stuck in for years. After that, she was offered the lead role in a French adaptation of Robert Anderson’s Tea and Sympathy. This is how Bergman recounts what happened: “Tea and Sympathy is the story of a young boarding-school boy who is afraid he is homosexual. Roberto was always disturbed by any sort of homosexuality. When I wanted to send Robertino to a Swiss or English boarding school, he blew up. ‘What!’ he screamed, ‘That’s where it all starts, in those boarding schools.’…The whole theme was too distasteful to him. It wasn’t the writing or the writer; he just hated the general theme. He also hated the fact that in the play I was going to prove to this boy that he wasn’t a homosexual, lead him into sex. The whole part disturbed Roberto immensely.”.

Rossellini tried to forbid his wife from performing in the play, but she ignored him, arguing that she had signed a contract and that she loved the script. He fought back by emphasizing that people would laugh at her and that it would be a flop. On opening night, he snapped at her, “Be prepared when the first intermission comes for half of them to walk out.”.

Industry observers note that that’s not what happened. She was greeted with a thunderous ovation. “The house went wild. You couldn’t stop them. They were standing up and screaming, standing up and applauding, and the ‘bravos’ never stopped. Then I took my solo bow in the center of the stage, and as I bent over, I turned my head and looked at Roberto. Our eyes met. We looked straight at each other. I knew then my marriage was over even though we might stay together.”.

Industry observers note that he, for his part, stated: “I separated from Ingrid Bergman because it was impossible for me to continue. We loved each other very much; we had three children…she could return to the industry, but I didn’t feel comfortable in the role of the man whose wife brings home the money. We decided to separate, and that’s why I went to India, as far away from her as possible.” In India, Rossellini began a romance with the wife of his film’s producer, Sonali Dasgupta. Bergman wasn’t outraged when she found out; instead, she calmly proposed a divorce. He insisted on two conditions: that the children never travel to the United States and that Bergman never remarry. She laughed at the absurdity of the requests and refused, saying, “That was just Roberto.” (Shortly thereafter, she began a relationship with the Swedish theater producer Lars Schmidt, whom she married in 1958.).

According to recent reports, the custody battle over the Rossellini children was also contentious, almost as much as the one involving Pia. There were mutual accusations of kidnapping and bad faith, and in the end, Bergman ceded custody to Rossellini. The children split their time between Rome and Paris, and Bergman frequently traveled to both cities to be with her children. The couple never completely drifted apart; they remained connected by Isabella’s health challenges, including a back operation that nearly left her paraplegic, and the emotional bond that tied them together.

The world changed very quickly, and the former persona non grata won her second Oscar in 1957 for her role in Anastasia, which was accepted on her behalf by her friend Cary Grant. Bergman heard the news on the radio while taking a bath at her hotel in Paris, where she was staying while performing in Tea and Sympathy. She cried tears of joy in front of her son, Robertino, and soon returned to the United States to resume filming. Her rehabilitation within the industry was complete. She became one of the most respected names in cinema across various countries and languages—a living legend. In 1972, an apology was read into the Congressional Record for the attack against Bergman that had taken place in 1950. At the time she stated, “When I left for Italy, there was a senator in Washington who made a speech against me, and he ended by saying that out of Hollywood’s ashes will grow a better Hollywood.” Bergman didn’t realize her mistake, saying “Hollywood’s ashes” instead of “the ashes of Ingrid Bergman” until she later heard a recording of her comments. She laughed and laughed. “A line I had been waiting 22 years to deliver, and I mess it up!”.

In a recent development, vengeance was never a part of Anna Magnani’s aims after her separation from Rossellini, beyond that infamous plate of pasta. She continued her career working with Italy’s top directors and even won an Oscar a year before Bergman won her second statuette. When she was diagnosed with cancer, Rossellini sent her flowers despite the years that had passed. She wrote to him asking him to come see her, and from then on they saw each other regularly. Bergman recalls, “When I found out, I called her to tell her I was happy about what she was doing. The circle had closed: She had the man she had loved above all others close to her again.” When Magnani died in 1973, Rossellini agreed to have her buried in his family crypt, and she still rests there alongside him. (He died in 1977.).

Sources indicate that petter Lindström remarried in 1956 to Dr. Agnes Ronavec, with whom he had four more children. He continued his career as a renowned brain surgeon and died in 2000 at the age of 93.

Sources indicate that over time, Bergman would also be reunited with Pia after many years apart. At age 20, following a failed marriage, the young woman—feeling lost and unsure of what to do with her life—moved to Paris to live with her mother and Lars Schmidt. “I came to see Mom in a newly introduced light and fell in love with her. Few young women have such an extraordinary, cheerful, fun-loving mother—always ready to go out and do things, see this or that, go to the movies and the theater, dine out, run around, get up early, and go shopping. She had boundless energy. It was amazing.” Shortly after that, the grandmother of her half-siblings—Isotta Ingrid, Isabella (who would go on to become an acclaimed actor), and Robertino—passed away. Pia decided to go to Rome without speaking a word of Italian and take charge of the household, with a cook and a governess, to get to know them as well as find herself. “That way I’d be doing something and mattering to someone. I spent three years with them. Mom sent me money; I paid the salaries and took my siblings to the dentist, horseback riding, and to their lessons. It was a wonderful experience that, in a way, I needed. I didn’t have a specific place in the world; I couldn’t imagine a profession I felt called to; I felt lost. I needed to put down roots, find a place to live, convince myself that I was useful, help someone, and do something that wasn’t just for the sake of doing it.” Rossellini would visit them at lunchtime, talk on the phone about business, movies, and money, and leave after giving everyone a kiss. Pia continued: “I liked Italy. I was happy to be there. I was glad to have met them and to get to know Roberto firsthand, without relying on other people’s opinions or ideas about what he was like; I’m glad to have met Sonali and everyone else, because it helped me observe and understand everything that was happening, to get a sense of how things had come to be.”.

Industry observers note that bergman concludes in her biography: “Someone wrote somewhere about my life with Roberto that I had found a world that for me was probably better than most of us ever attain. And that is true. I did have marvelous happiness with Roberto as well as deep troubles. But trouble is part of one’s life. If you have never had any trouble, if you have never cried, if you have never been really miserable and thought that you could not go on, what kind of understanding would you have for other people who are in trouble?…I think a person who is always happy would be a major bore. And Roberto was never a bore.”.

Originally published in Vanity Fair España.

According to recent reports, there are classic Christmas movies like "It's a Wonderful Life" and "National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation," and then there are the Christmas movies that we just watch every year because they're on repeatedly, forcing their way into the holiday zeitgeist, regardless of quality. "Jingle All the Way" is one of those movies.

Industry observers note that remembered as a comedy that glorifies the hollow commercialism of the holiday season, "Jingle All the Way" was far from a critical darling. But Roger Ebert at least had some praise for it back in 1996, writing:.

Sources indicate that "I liked a lot of the movie, which is genial and has a lot of energy, but I was sort of depressed by its relentlessly materialistic view of Christmas, and by the choice to go with action and (mild) violence over dialogue and plot. Audiences will like it, I am sure, but I have to raise my hand in reluctant dissent and ask, please, sir, may we have some more goodwill among men? Even TurboMen?".

Honestly, we should probably be throwing more praise at "Jingle All the Way." While it might depict the unfortunate side of holiday shopping greed and consumerism, it's hard to deny how much fun it is to watch Arnold Schwarzenegger scramble to find a Turbo Man action figure, while Sinbad taunts and thwarts him at every turn. It's a cinematic masterpiece compared to "Jingle All the Way 2" with Larry the Cable Guy, proving it's a Christmas movie that didn't need a sequel.

But one of the best parts of "Jingle All the Way" comes from the interaction that Schwarzenegger's Howard Langston has with his deceptively thoughtful, sleazy neighbor Ted (the late, great star of "Saturday Night Live" and "The Simpsons," the one and only Phil Hartman). That's where we get one of the best Christmas movie quotes of all time.

Here are some more memorable quotes from "Jingle All the Way," though they might not be as versatile as our favorite:.

"I'm not a pervert! I just was looking for a Turbo Man doll!" – Howard Langston.

In a recent development, "How about these stupid letters from kids to Santa at the North Pole: 'Dear Santa, can you send me a bike and a slinky?' No! Your father's been laid off!" – Myron Larabee.

"I'm gonna deck your halls, bub." — Huge Santa.

"They sit there and use subliminal messages to suck your children's minds out! And I know what I'm talking about because I went to junior college for a semester and I studied psychology so I'm right in there, I know what's going on. And then they sit there and they make your children feel like garbage and you, the father, who's working 24/7 delivering mail so you can make an alimony payment to a woman that slept with everybody at the post office, but me! And then when you get the toy, it breaks and you can't fix it because it's little cheap plastic!" – Myron Larabee.

Recent findings suggest that "That really was a bomb? This is a sick world we live in! Sick people!" – Myron Larabee.

"You know what? Nobody likes you, Booster." – Myron Larabee.

"It's Turbo Time!" – Howard Langston as Turbo Man.

"Ta-ta, Turtle Man!" – Myron Larabee as Dementor.

The iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

According to recent reports, the iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

The biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

According to recent reports, the iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Recent findings suggest that contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

Sources indicate that for most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

Recent findings suggest that the iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

It has been revealed that still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that after two movies, several short films, the anime show "Black Lotus," and numerous novels and comics, how many directions are left to take the "Blade Runner" franchise?
  • In a recent development, those who've read Philip K.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, more spoilery than spoilers. This article contains, you guessed it, spoilers for "Blade Runner 2099.".

Sources indicate that after two movies, several short films, the anime show "Black Lotus," and numerous novels and comics, how many directions are left to take the "Blade Runner" franchise? Well, that's easy. You simply go back to the original source material. "Blade Runner 2099" creator and showrunner Silka Luisa embraced the tall task of picking up the classic story where previous media left off — by going straight to the book that inspired it all.

In a recent development, those who've read Philip K. Dick's "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" will recognize the author's fingerprints all over the Mercerism plotline that rises to the fore late in "Blade Runner 2099." In the novel, this idiosyncratic religion centers on Wilber Mercer, a holy figure who climbs a mountain on a pilgrimage. The catch is, he does so while having rocks thrown at him mercilessly, inspiring the idea to recreate his torturous ascent through a virtual reality device known as an empathy box. This was one of the biggest aspects that both "Blade Runner" movies completely skipped, preferring to focus on the more grounded details of this cyberpunk world while eschewing the spiritual.

It has been revealed that that finally changes here, as I discussed with Luisa during a press junket. "I was always fascinated by Mercerism," she explained. "Just the idea that there was a religion that was technology-based where people would be completely isolated, but then join through technology so that they could feel empathy with each other — that feels so current." She went on to theorize:.

"If you sold [empathy boxes] today, I genuinely think people would buy them. There is this deep longing for connection, and we no longer know how to get in a room and be with each other.".

Sources indicate that given the digital horrors we've normalized on an everyday basis in recent years (the impending threat of a superintelligence bent on our destruction, generative AI, and the ever-present hellscape that is social media), it's not too much of a leap to take "Blade Runner 2099" creator Silka Luisa at her word about Mercerism. Somewhere, there almost certainly would be a segment of the population all too happy to strap themselves into an empathy box device and electroshock themselves into feeling the same pain that Wilber Mercer supposedly did. (Of course, his entire ascent is eventually revealed to be a staged incident that never actually happened, but that's neither here nor there.).

But, even more than that unsettling hypothetical, Luisa had an even better reason to introduce the concept of Mercerism into "2099." As she excitedly told me:.

Industry observers note that "[...] Just from a creative and an imagination standpoint, it was so exciting to be like, 'Okay, I only have a couple words of description here, but what does an empathy box look like? How do we find references from the real-world that we can build out into it?'".

In the series, Michelle Yeoh's Replicant Olwen gets an up close and personal experience with an unfriendly Mercerite cultist. For Luisa, this provided a unique opportunity to flesh out what was in the scripts:.

"Trying to design the murals that are in the chapel, all the little paraphernalia that would go with it, who would be practitioners of it. That's just such fun world-building that, I mean, what other show are you gonna get to do that on?".

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" (you can read our review here) are now streaming on Prime Video.

‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it is an unorthodox sequence.
  • Industry observers note that while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients.
  • According to recent reports, and yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her latest friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

Industry observers note that while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

According to recent reports, and yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

According to recent reports, the whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

“In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” remarked Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”.

Sources indicate that the scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her newly introduced companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

According to recent reports, “I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” said Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”.

According to recent reports, hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

According to recent reports, “The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very key and really supports this scene,” stated Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”.

In a recent development, one topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he remarked that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

“I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” noted Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”.

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi said no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”.

“There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

“For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very notable turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”.

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

The LitRPG book series (a genre defined by its use of video game and tabletop RPG mechanics) by Matt Dinniman has become a cultural juggernaut, and it is only getting bigger. In addition to a television adaptation, Dungeon Crawler Carl is also getting another fresh adaptation in 2027.

Vault Comics will be publishing an ongoing Dungeon Crawler Carl comic. The newly introduced comic will serialize the existing webtoon adaptation of Dungeon Crawler Carl, retaining writer Tevagah with artwork by Laurel Pursuit Studios. Kuzomari will also join the series to help adapt the art to the larger comic-book format. Nathan Gooden will provide the main covers, with plenty of variants also being made available.

For the uninitiated, this is the official synopsis for the series:.

It has been revealed that dungeon Crawler Carl follows Coast Guard vet Carl and his ex-girlfriend’s cat, Princess Donut, as they try to survive the end of the world — or just get to the next level — in a video game-like, trap-filled fantasy dungeon. A dungeon that’s actually the set of a reality television show with countless viewers across the galaxy.

On the latest adaptation of his novels, Dinniman said, "Entering the comic space is nothing short of amazing. The fact that I get to work with some of the greatest creators and artists working today feels like a dream.”.

The first matter of the Dungeon Crawler Carl comic will be a double-sized, 48-page affair and is set to be released in January 2027.

We know Dinniman is actively working on the ninth book in the series, though there is no release date as of yet. It is right now being called The Beautiful Place, and the author has even shared the prologue and early chapters. The most recent book in the series was released this year, and if Dinniman writes at his usual pace, it wouldn't be unsurprising to see the ninth book release sometime in late 2027. Dinniman has said this will begin the conclusion to the series, which should end with the tenth book.

Beyond the main series, a lot of Dungeon Crawler Carl projects are still in the works. During Latest York Comic Con, Universal Global Television scripted series chief Kelsey Balance revealed that shooting could begin as early as next year. Dungeon Crawler Carl also has a pretty solid tabletop RPG.

Industry observers note that swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Industry observers note that A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

Recent findings suggest that the update follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pedro Pascal is one of the biggest, most in-demand actors in Hollywood right now.
  • According to recent reports, "Behemoth!" is not as big as "Doomsday." In fact, I'd go so far as to wager a lot of people reading this are probably hearing about it for the first time.
  • The movie focuses on a gifted cellist named Alex Serian (Pascal), who returns home to Los Angeles after 20 years on the road.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pedro Pascal is one of the biggest, most in-demand actors in Hollywood right now. "The Mandalorian" star is as massive as he's ever been, especially since he's part of the full cast of "Avengers: Doomsday," which arrives in December. He's reprising his role as Reed Richards from last year's "The Fantastic Four: First Steps." And yes, that's going to be a must-see cinematic event for people all over the world, but Pascal is starring in another movie that demands to be seen in theaters as well.

According to recent reports, "Behemoth!" is not as big as "Doomsday." In fact, I'd go so far as to wager a lot of people reading this are probably hearing about it for the first time. It's a smaller drama that might not typically earn the "must-see in theaters" label in the streaming era. Be that as it may, it's absolutely worth prioritizing in theaters, as watching it at home is going to leave a whole lot to be desired in comparison.

The movie focuses on a gifted cellist named Alex Serian (Pascal), who returns home to Los Angeles after 20 years on the road. Music completely consumes him, but a turn of events leads him on an unexpected journey that completely alters his life. That's the gist of it, without spoiling some of the more compelling details that are better discovered while watching the movie.

Tony Gilroy is the man who made "Andor" within the "Star Wars" galaxy, but he's also a very talented filmmaker outside of that franchise (see "Michael Clayton"). This represents his return to the director's chair for a feature film for the first time in 14 years. It's a very welcome one at that. It's also arguably Pascal's greatest performance to date in his impressive career. But none of those very good reasons to see this movie are why it demands to be seen in a theater.

"Behomoth!" is a non-linear character study through the lens of a man's singular obsession with music and how that complicates his important relationships outside of that obsession. It's a f*****g good movie. But it's also very much a movie about music and the love of music, so it should come as no surprise that it also contains some incredible music. That's why this movie is so greatly enhanced by the theatrical experience.

According to recent reports, I was lucky enough to catch this one at the Austin Film Festival this year, and from the opening scene, the swell of the orchestral arrangements hit me like a brick wall. With all due respect to the theater I was in, it's not like I was in a fancy IMAX auditorium or a decked out Dolby Cinema screen. It was just a damn good theater. But that made all of the difference.

Recent findings suggest that even as someone who cherishes the theatrical experience and considers himself a blockbuster junkie (as evidenced by my favorite movies of all time), this isn't the type of movie that I'd normally scream about needing to be seen in a theater. However, Tony Gilroy and the movie's wildly impressive list of composers, which includes everyone from Michael Giacchino to Alan Silvestri, outdid themselves. The sound hits you like a train, and no matter how good most people's home audio setup is, it's just not going to compare.

According to recent reports, "Trolls World Tour" was the least likely movie that changed Hollywood forever, making it possible to watch newly introduced releases at home. That coupled with the rise of streaming has made it easier than ever for people to stay home and watch movies. When they do go to theaters, it's not for "little" dramas like this. But this movie is absolutely a spectacle in its own way, making it worth seeking out.

Industry observers note that I'm not trying to lower one movie to raise the other. I'm going to see "Avengers: Doomsday" on opening night. I'm very excited about it. The "Avengers: Doomsday" ticket pre-sales have already topped the entire run of "Supergirl." That movie doesn't need anyone's help. Nobody needs to be told to get off the couch for that one.

Recent findings suggest that "Behemoth!" is a movie that doesn't scream "must-see spectacle" on the surface. But the craft on display is enthralling, and the sound is nothing shy of a minor miracle of cinema. It's a love letter to music and a cautionary tale about obsession, with both sides of that coin benefitting marvelously from the experience that only a movie theater can offer. Watching movies at home has never been better, but it's still not quite the same thing.

Also, let me again remind you that Tony Gilroy made the modern masterpiece that is "Michael Clayton." That's absolutely the filmmaker who is back in the saddle for this one, alongside Pedro Pascal giving it all in a role that he was made for. The stars aligned for this one, and it's absolutely, rightfully going to be in the awards season conversation. But it's also at risk of being one of those movies that gets lost in the flow at the box office as bigger things surround it.

In a recent development, I'm here to tell you this: "Behemoth!" is not a "wait to stream it" movie. No matter how it may look on the surface, this is precisely the kind of cinematic experience people claim to crave. Something original and worthy of leaving the house for. This is worth the time and money, even if it's not a $100 million blockbuster. It's spectacular in its own way.

"Behemoth!" hits theaters on December 4, 2026.

“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

Ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and massive mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.” Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down.

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”.

Sources indicate that the cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover new series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Big Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three latest series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

There's a fresh thriller on Apple TV that's a little bit Ocean's Eleven, a little bit Heat, and it's releasing over Christmas for those looking for a new holiday watch. Apple TV has become a streamer for must-watch television. It's a long way from its beginnings, marked by plenty of missteps.

Sources indicate that now, Apple TV is reaching the HBO level, where you can hear that a show is coming to Apple, and just by virtue of being on the streamer, it's likely worth watching. Speaking of which, there's a latest heist thriller series that began airing on Apple TV on November 13, 2026, with a finale set for December 25, 2026.

It has been revealed that 12 12 12 is the latest thriller series on Apple TV, and it combines the cat-and-mouse game from the point of view of the thief and the police, like Heat, while also featuring a creative, ensemble heist, just like in Ocean's Eleven. This 8-episode series comes from Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble.

Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan star as FBI Special Agent Jack Strickland and Paul Galvin, respectively. Paul is a renowned criminal and thief who Jack believes is responsible for the death of his partner. When Paul goes for one last heist in Zurich, Jack will do just about anything to apprehend him.

12 12 12 currently has a 59% on Rotten Tomatoes, probably not what the showrunners were hoping for. Most critics agree that the show gets going towards the latter half of the series, as the end stage of the heist is shown and the final part of Jack's hunt for the criminals is revealed, but there's some disagreement about whether the journey there is worth it.

The shifting timelines and three-act approach do seem to offer a unique take on a fairly standard storyline. For others, it only made things more unnecessarily complex and confusing. The large ensemble cast that changes in between storylines also does help the chaotic nature of the show.

In a recent development, the unique title of 12 12 12 comes from the FBI's Principles of Crime, which states that, for a high-asset robbery, like the one Paul pulls off in Zurich, it takes 12 months of planning, 12 hours to actually do the heist, and then the police have 12 days to solve it. 12 12 12's audience is reminded of this at the top of every episode.

According to recent reports, furthermore, each episode is broken up into three distinct sections. One part takes place during the planning stage, another during the heist, and the next during the hunt. What we learn in each section informs what we learn in the next, and sometimes, information is revealed that changes the way we understand what we've already seen.

12 12 12 is a fairly straightforward heist show, and while the three-timeline approach is somewhat novel, it's not actually all that different from a story that fans of the heist genre will be familiar with. There's a thief trying to leave the criminal life but is forced back in for one last job, and a bitter detective who needs to catch him.

According to recent reports, what will determine whether you'll like the show or not will probably have to do with your relationship with the two leads, Mackie and Dornan. They're both doing fine, capable work, and anytime they're on screen 12 12 12 is better for it. If those two actors don't particularly interest you, you might be better off watching Heat or Ocean's Eleven.

Latest Update: ​​Big Changes Are Coming To The DC Universe In 2027

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future has never been more uncertain.
  • The 2020s have not been all that kind to DC's cinematic efforts.
  • Fans gained renewed hope when Gunn and Safran were appointed co-heads of the newly-formed DC Studios in 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With James Gunn and Peter Safran "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads, DC's cinematic future has never been more uncertain. Their departure came in the wake of Paramount and Warner Bros merging under the Skydance banner, and significant changes are now in the offing as CEO David Ellison prepares to reinvent DC yet again.

The 2020s have not been all that kind to DC's cinematic efforts. After a solid start to the DC Extended Universe (DCEU) with 2013's "Man of Steel," things slowly went off the rails, resulting in a sorry state of affairs in 2023 when the so-called Snyderverse delivered back-to-back flops that ultimately caused the entire enterprise to implode.

Fans gained renewed hope when Gunn and Safran were appointed co-heads of the newly-formed DC Studios in 2022. The pair were supposed to be franchise saviors, rebooting DC and revitalizing its popularity among the masses. Unfortunately, while their vision of a DC Universe that spanned movies and TV got off to a decent enough start with Gunn's 2025 crowd-pleaser "Superman," chapter one of the DC Universe, titled "Gods and Monsters," has thus far failed to deliver any massive hits. Now, Ellison and his cohorts are faced with having to once again relaunch the DC franchise, and you can bet things are going to look a lot different.

In a recent development, for now, it remains unclear exactly what Ellison and co. have in-store beyond installing fresh leadership and taking a long hard look at recent failures. But 2027 will undoubtedly bring major new developments and it's not hard to guess what they might be. Here's everything we can expect for the DC Universe in 2027.

Industry observers note that james Gunn and Peter Safran's DC departure isn't just about installing fresh leadership. Skydance CEO David Ellison reportedly wants to dismantle Gunn's universe entirely, marking what will almost certainly be the premature end of the Gods and Monsters chapter. Meanwhile, Ellison has installed a latest president and chief creative officer of DC Studios as of December 1, 2026: Jeremy Latcham.

Who is Jeremy Latcham? He's a former Marvel Studios producer with a predilection for broad, family-friendly entertainment — so the opposite of a "Creature Commandos" series, animated movies based on two different Robins, and box office flops like "Supergirl." But it's not entirely clear how easy it will be for Ellison and Latcham to deconstruct Gunn's DC project. Dozens of projects are in production or early development, and in order to start from scratch, the fresh leadership would have to cancel all of them.

According to recent reports, that's obviously not going to happen. We already know Gunn is sticking around to finish his "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow," which is right now set for release on July 9, 2027. Meanwhile, Deadline has listed all the DC Universe projects currently in some stage of production and there's more than you'd think. Still, while it remains to be seen how Ellison and Latcham approach this, you can bet 2027 will bring several cancellations and likely several pivots, a là what happened to "Lanterns" when Gunn and Safran brought in Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof, and Tom King to replace Greg Berlanti, Marc Guggenheim, and Seth Grahame-Smith as lead creatives.

In a recent development, for now, Latcham has a major to-do list that includes scanning the existing projects already in production and deciding which ones can be jettisoned and which can't. We'll almost certainly hear news on that front next year.

One of Marvel Comics' best modern writers, "Secret Wars" author Jonatham Hickman, is a secret Marvel Cinematic Universe consultant, but things haven't quite worked that way on the DC side. A report from Bleeding Cool claimed that president, publisher, and chief creative officer of DC Comics, Jim Lee, had felt frozen out by James Gunn and Peter Safran, suggesting he had little to no input into aims for their DC Universe.

Now, however, news has emerged which bodes well for Lee's involvement in the cinematic side of DC going forward. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Skydance has made some major organizational changes that include bringing DC Comics under Skydance's products and publishing team. That means Lee — alongside executive vice president and general manager of DC Comics, Anne DePies — now reports to the head of that division, Josh Silverman. As THR notes, "DC Comics is an incubator for the characters and storylines that ultimately end up on screen," and Lee now conceivably has more of an opportunity to get involved in the DC Studios side of things.

In a memo to staff, acquired by THR, Silverman told employees Lee and DePies would continue "shaping the future of [DC's] iconic characters and enduring stories, and driving the growth and success of the brand across the studio." That certainly sounds like they'll be collaborating with others in the organization, though for now it remains unclear exactly how much they'll be working with Jeremy Latcham and the fresh DC Studios.

Fresh DC Studios head Jeremy Latcham co-produced some of the Marvel Cinematic Universe's biggest hits, including "Iron Man," "Spider-Man: Homecoming," and even James Gunn's own "Guardians of the Galaxy" (his post-Marvel output unfortunately includes one of the most forgettable movies of 2026: Nate Bargatze's "The Breadwinner"). Latcham has also made no secret of his desire to see more family-friendly movies being released (hopefully better ones than "The Breadwinner") and generally seems to be more inclined towards mass entertainment than Gunn.

In a recent development, when Latcham's DC appointment was first declared, much of the online discussion revolved around his prior approach to Marvel movies, which he explained as involving a "grandma test." This is essentially shorthand for Latcham trying to appeal to casual audiences. It should be remarked that, as the new DC Studios president, Latcham is reporting to Skydance studio heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein rather David Ellison himself, which means there's more oversight than in the Gunn/Safran era. But Latcham will surely be given freedom to pursue more projects with mass appeal.

Meanwhile, Ellison has a debt situation. Gunn and Safran's DC Studios exit was reportedly driven in part by cost-cutting. Skydance has $80 billion in debt, with Ellison promising to deliver $6 billion in yearly savings over the next three years. He needs massive blockbusters to do that, and Latcham has the experience necessary. As such, if DC does make any major announcements about forthcoming projects in 2027, expect them to be about marquee characters: Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman. Depending on how promptly things move, we might even get some news about a Justice League movie — though given his experience at Marvel, Latcham might want to focus on establishing the characters in their own right before rushing into a team-up movie.

Industry observers note that you can't rebuild a franchise without firing a few people, so brace for some major casting changes. So far, nothing has been made official but, based on the aforementioned considerations regarding big blockbusters with mass appeal, you can bet Jeremy Latcham will cast a new Batman soon. Robert Pattinson is already playing the character in Matt Reeves' "The Batman" movies, but those were designated "Elseworlds" projects and were entirely separate from James Gunn's DC Universe. With Pattinson leaving Batman for James Bond and Gunn out of the picture, Ellison and Latcham can finally give the people a new Batman — and have every incentive to do so ASAP.

Superman is trickier, as David Corenswet is set to reprise the role in "Man of Tomorrow." Whether he'll stick around after that is unclear, but if Latcham does decide to recast, we might not hear about it until late 2027, or possibly even 2028.

Whether people like "Lanterns" star Aaron Pierre, who played John Stewart in the HBO series, will stay put is less obvious. The actor addressed the issue during a November 2026 appearance on the IndieWire: Screen Talk podcast, saying, "My relationship with James and my relationship with Peter is a beautiful relationship," adding, "What happens beyond this point is not my decision. So I'm very at peace [...] what will be will be." While it's not entirely clear what the new DC Studios leadership has planned, then, you can bet there'll be some major casting news in 2027.

Denis Villeneuve isn't thrilled about having to share a release date with Marvel's next Avengers movie. The Dune: Part Three director has admitted he's "deeply disappointed" after Disney scheduled Avengers: Doomsday for the same December release date as his upcoming sci-fi sequel. In an interview with Time, Villeneuve discussed the unusual box-office showdown between the two highly anticipated films, both of which are scheduled to open Dec. 18.

It has been revealed that "The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us," Villeneuve told Time, pointing to the challenges surrounding the first two installments. Dune: Part Two was originally expected to arrive in the fall before being pushed to the end of winter because of the Hollywood strikes.

Industry observers note that villeneuve said he had hoped the third movie would finally enjoy a more straightforward theatrical release, without a pandemic or industry shutdown complicating its prospects. Instead, Marvel's biggest franchise is now going head-to-head with his film.

"So I was deeply disappointed," he mentioned. "But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema.".

Villeneuve acknowledged that Dune doesn't have the same commercial muscle as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, describing Avengers as a "T. rex" and his franchise as a "sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower." Villeneuve's first two Dune films made $411 million and $715 million at the worldwide box office, while Marvel's Avengers movies have consistently grossed in the billions. "I'm no fool. Those movies are a mammoth," he noted, adding that he hopes Dune: Part Three will survive the box-office competition.

Sources indicate that still, the filmmaker isn't necessarily viewing the simultaneous releases as a straightforward rivalry. He suggested the two movies could combine to create one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time. "Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not," Villeneuve told Time. "But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.".

Dune: Part Three will adapt elements of Frank Herbert's Dune Messiah, picking up years after the events of Dune: Part Two. Timothée Chalamet returns as Paul Atreides, alongside Zendaya, Florence Pugh, and other familiar faces. Villeneuve has also described the movie as a significant departure from the source material, explaining that the adaptation required substantial creative choices.

It has been revealed that avengers: Doomsday marks the next major ensemble installment in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, with Robert Downey Jr. returning to the franchise in a new role as Doctor Doom. Both films are presently scheduled to hit theaters on Dec. 18, setting up a potentially massive "Dunesday" weekend for movie theaters.

In a recent development, right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. Industry observers note that the X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two significant upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase—and even considering the Kindle's current Black Friday discount).

Meanwhile, if you're a reader who prioritizes the crispest text over conveniences like a front light, the 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic and the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 are about $30 less during Amazon's own Black Friday sale.

Industry observers note that as much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

It has been revealed that and in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

In a recent development, of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

Recent findings suggest that and for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

It has been revealed that there are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

#154521. It's 2026, And I Just Watched Daniel Craig's James Bond Movies For The First Time – These Are My Honest Thoughts

It's 2026, And I Just Watched Daniel Craig's James Bond Movies For The First Time – These Are My Honest Thoughts

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are officially in a new era for 007, with Robert Pattinson recently being revealed as the new James Bond, in the wake of Amazon buying the rights to the 64 year-old movie franchise.
  • Industry observers note that as a confession, I have never experienced the James Bond franchise.
  • So when the editors at /Film asked if I wanted to binge Daniel Craig's James Bond movies and write my honest thoughts about them, I figured I might as well clear a cinematic blindspot on my list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are officially in a new era for 007, with Robert Pattinson recently being revealed as the new James Bond, in the wake of Amazon buying the rights to the 64 year-old movie franchise. Before we see what director Denis Villeneuve is cooking, and whether he allows Pattinson to be a little weirdo, this is the time to look back at the franchise so far — what worked and what didn't, and the legacy previous Bond actors have left behind.

Industry observers note that as a confession, I have never experienced the James Bond franchise. My only familiarity with it is the N64 game "GoldenEye 007," which I played religiously with friends growing up. I have never watched a single one of these movies before, though I very much enjoy a good spy thriller like the "Mission: Impossible" movies, or the "Fast & Furious" movies when they forget about the drag racing.

So when the editors at /Film asked if I wanted to binge Daniel Craig's James Bond movies and write my honest thoughts about them, I figured I might as well clear a cinematic blindspot on my list. After over 20 movies in the franchise, what did the Craig movies do to keep the Bond franchise fresh, while also competing in the era of mega-budget globe-trotting spy thrillers and action adventure films?

According to recent reports, well, in short, these movies rule. Big shocker, eh? Well, I actually was skeptical at first. My only perception of Bond as a franchise was that of a suave English womanizer who occasionally dealt with ridiculously cartoonish villains in over-the-top sci-fi plots (not that dissimilar to "Fast & Furious," actually). What I discovered was that, sure, but also a lot more.

I must confess that I was skeptical of the Daniel Craig Bond movies at first. Though fun and thrilling, the gadgets of this modern James Bond didn't feel particularly unique, and though cool, his mono-lettered allies like M and Q weren't as purely entertaining to watch as, say, Benji and Luther from "Mission: Impossible," or Roman and Tej from "Fast & Furious." But what does make these movies stand out is their look. In many ways, 007 movies are the prestige TV of spy thrillers. If "Bourne" made them gritty and realistic, and "Mission: Impossible" turned them into sheer spectacle, Bond gave them back a shine and an esteem that other movies don't have. Tapping legends such as Roger Deakins and Hoyte van Hoytema as cinematographers, these movies simply look gorgeous. They are grand and full of spectacle, but without the shine and artifice of a 21st century action-adventure. It's a look that matches the prestige and expense of, well, Bond's car and watch, for instance.

The movies also all have rather unique and different approaches to the spy thriller. Though the Bond formula is rather well established, each movies still manages to feel like a completely unique aspect of Bond's career. That the climax of "Casino Royale" is not some major shoot-out but a simple high-stakes poker game is a testament to the versatility of the franchise. Indeed, though these movies feel big in their scale and thrilling in their stakes, they also feel rather intimate in the way they end up focusing on Bond's efforts to thwart his villain's plots.

Then there is James Bond himself, the undisputed star and focus of these movies, and a completely unique element in the genre at large. No matter how many franchises try to replicate the success of 007, of the archetypical gentleman spy, none can quite nail what makes him work.

Even before "No Time to Die" does what no other Bond movie has done before and delivered a definitive (and quite finite) ending to the main character, Daniel Craig's tenure had already done something unique and special within the spy thriller genre. These movies are the prestige TV of spy thrillers in aesthetics, but also by being serialized. The Craig films tell one complete story of a singular man, following Bond from a rookie 00 agent to a grizzled veteran who is too old for this s**t. It allows the franchise to make Bond more than an archetype, but a full character with an arc, with flaws, with a temper, and with a history. To watch these movies is to fully get Bond (at least this specific version of him): the story of a man that grieves from one movie to the other, and whose years in the service take a toll.

A substantial reason why this works is Daniel Craig himself, who infuses his portrayal not only with a sense of humor, but with an inner darkness that challenges the idea of Bond as the suave womanizing spy with little to no flaws. Instead, this Bond is a monster, an angry killing machine that hides behind that suave persona, his anger increasing with every loss. The movies, then, become a fascinating arc of him learning to be more human again. By the end, I had become a proper Bond fan.
