📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that across the entire live-action Transformers franchise, there are just some designs that will never be beaten.
  • Since the 80s and the original animated series, characters like Optimus Prime, Bumblebee, and Megatron have had very distinct looks both in animation and as physical toys.
  • Keeping that in mind, here are 8 of the most perfect, 10/10 live-action Transformers designs we absolutely love, based on pure cool factor, unique appearances that just work, and/or excellent live-action translations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that across the entire live-action Transformers franchise, there are just some designs that will never be beaten. Without a doubt, Michael Bay changed the game in 2007 with the start of his live-action series, breathing fresh life into the entire Transformers franchise as a whole. Part of that includes some of the raddest live-action robots to ever be seen on the big-screen.

Since the 80s and the original animated series, characters like Optimus Prime, Bumblebee, and Megatron have had very distinct looks both in animation and as physical toys. As a result, translating those iconic depictions to live-action was always going to be one of the biggest hurdles to getting audiences on board. That said, very few live-action Transformers designs look bad, and a select few have certainly achieved GOAT-status.

Keeping that in mind, here are 8 of the most perfect, 10/10 live-action Transformers designs we absolutely love, based on pure cool factor, unique appearances that just work, and/or excellent live-action translations.

Without question, Devastator is one of the most ambitious and intimidating designs in the live-action Transformers franchise, largely due to the sheer scale of the massive Decepticon. Formed from six different Constructicons (just like in the original animated series), Devastator is a huge Combiner who debuted in 2009's Revenge of the Fallen, deployed by Megatron in Egypt to uncover the giant Star Harvester hidden within the Great Pyramid of Giza.

Industry observers note that rather than combining from construction vehicles that are all the same green-and-purple color, each piece of Devastator is mismatched with various colors, along with a gaping maw of a mouth and multiple eyes. As such, the industrial monster that is Devastator has one of the scariest and most intimidating live-action Decepticon designs, despite his limited screen time in the Transformers franchise.

Industry observers note that also debuting in Revenge of the Fallen, Sideswipe is one of the sleekest Autobots in the live-action movies. Transforming into a silver Chevrolet Corvette Stingray, Sideswipe's most notable design feature in his robot form is two car wheels positioned as his feet like roller skates, allowing him to move across a battlefield with more fluid motion than most of his fellow Autobots. He also has large blades on his arms, making his distinct fighting style even more of a unique threat to the Decepticons.

Recent findings suggest that debuting in 2014's Age of Extinction, Crosshairs' chosen vehicle form is notably a later-model Chevrolet Corvette Stingray, having a shared vehicle form with Sideswipe in the earlier Transformers films, with a green color scheme rather than silver. However, what makes Crosshairs so awesome is that he arguably has one of the most stylish robot forms in the live-action Transformers franchise, having an effortlessly cool coat-like configuration of vehicle parts that very much adds to his gunslinger personality/aesthetic. Likewise, Crosshairs' dual pistols cement his role as an Autobot survivor/combat specialist.

Debuting in 2011's Dark of the Moon, Decepticon Shockwave has one of the coolest and most powerful designs in the live-action movies. Featuring a single eye just like his counterpart in the original animated series, the emotionless Shockwave on the big-screen commands his Driller pet, a huge Cybertronian beast made up of several devastatingly massive mechanical tentacles, making him one of the most formidable Decepticons in the entire franchise. While he doesn't receive nearly enough screen time in Dark of the Moon, Shockwave is easily one of the biggest and scariest threats.

In a recent development, debuting in the first live-action Transformers movie, Michael Bay's Megatron design is more original compared to his more traditional, G1 look. However, the unique design eventually became iconic in its own right and is certainly one of the most intimidating and fearsome-looking versions of the Decepticon leader across the franchise.

Sources indicate that having an incredibly angular and pointed appearance with jagged edges, sharp teeth, and clawed hands, Megatron is the epitome of a deadly weapon brought to life. Capable of turning into both a brutal tank and alien jet in the live-action movies, the Bayverse Megatron is a prime example of a design that has major cool factor points, despite its more original appearance.

As a major caveat to this list, it has to be noted that the brief Cybertron flashbacks in 2018's Bumblebee feature some of the coolest G1-inspired live-action designs, quick as they are. While it seems unfair to the entire live-action franchise to simply list all the bots seen in just a couple of minutes of screen time, personal bias compels me to at least include Soundwave.

Unlike the version seen in 2011's Dark of the Moon, the version of Soundwave seen in Bumblebee embraces everything that made his original G1 so awesome, including his monotone vocoder voice, blue-and-gray color scheme with yellow accents and red eyes, shoulder cannon, and chest compartment to launch his various cassette minions like Ravage and Laserbeak. A perfect combination of classic G1 appearance with more modern detailing, Soundwave's design in 2018's Bumblebee is easily one of the coolest and most satisfying when it comes to the live-action Decepticons.

Now we get to Bumblebee himself, who's easily one of the most vital bots in the entire Bayverse and beyond as Optimus Prime's loyal lieutenant who's also best friends with crucial human characters like Shia LaBeouf's Sam Witwicky and Hailee Steinfeld's Charlie Watson.

Bumblebee has gone through several different live-action designs with his classic yellow-and-black color scheme, starting with his epic Camaro vehicle forms that redefined the look of the character for a new generation of Transformers fans, complete with car-door "wings" on his back and a face shield with insectoid-like eyes to help add to his namesake. However, the classic Autobot's appearance in his 2018 solo movie arguably provides the best balance between G1 authenticity with a more classic 1967 Volkswagen Beetle vehicle form, while still keeping with the robot design established in the earlier Bayverse movies.

With slightly more rounded proportions thanks to his classic vehicle form, Bumblebee looks so good in his spin-off. However, that isn't to say he's ever looked bad in earlier movies or the Transformers films that followed with his truly awesome Camaro forms. Also, his expressive face does wonders for the character, who more often than not uses radio frequencies to speak to make up for his damaged voice. He's a true "heart of the franchise" character if ever there was one.

Recent findings suggest that it shouldn't come as a huge surprise that Optimus Prime ranks at the top of this list. As the noble leader of the Autobots, Optimus has arguably received the most attention of any character in the entire live-action Transformers franchise, and for good reason. While he's had many different forms and designs over the years with varying levels of authenticity to the classic G1 look, you really can't go wrong with the OG live-action that debuted with Michael Bay's first film back in 2007.

Optimus Prime's live-action debut was a major cinematic achievement, translating his classic semi-truck appearance into a mechanical form that felt both practical and natural in "real life." Featuring red flames and accents on a blue frame, Optimus' OG form still holds classic features like his iconic face shield and distinct head design, while still having a more complex and modernized form to best convey how a truck could indeed transform its parts into a massive robot body in live-action.

Not every Optimus Prime form has been universally loved (The Last Knight's wasn't great), and more recent versions like the Optimus seen in Bumblebee and Rise of the Beasts have embraced G1 aesthetics even further, which has been cool to see. Nevertheless, the Bayverse's OG design is arguably still the best for live-action Optimus Prime, and the most perfect 10/10 design for the entire Transformers franchise overall. Without such a solid look and design for Transformers' most central character and hero, I sincerely doubt the franchise would have done as well as it has.

Industry News: Magic: The Gathering Designer Reveals 2026’s 11 Best New Commanders

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With 2026 delivering a packed release schedule for Magic: The Gathering exploring classic planes and several Universes Beyond crossovers, Commander players have had plenty of exciting fresh legends to build around.
  • When Polygon spoke with Magic: The Gathering Principal Designer Gavin Verhey about the year's lineup at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, he walked through each major release to highlight what he considers some of 2026’s most powerful Commanders.
  • It has been revealed that we all love abilities that trigger when something enters the battlefield, don’t we?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With 2026 delivering a packed release schedule for Magic: The Gathering exploring classic planes and several Universes Beyond crossovers, Commander players have had plenty of exciting fresh legends to build around. From returning to familiar fantasy worlds in sets like Lorwyn Eclipsed and Secrets of Strixhaven to epic crossovers like Marvel Super Heroes, The Hobbit, and Star Trek, the year brought an unprecedented wave of Commanders for casual and competitive tables alike.

When Polygon spoke with Magic: The Gathering Principal Designer Gavin Verhey about the year's lineup at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, he walked through each major release to highlight what he considers some of 2026’s most powerful Commanders. Rather than focus strictly on raw power ceilings, Verhey pointed toward the legends that spark creative brewing, surprising table politics, and memorable gameplay moments across every 2026 release. Here's a look at this year's 11 best Commanders in the order they were released.

It has been revealed that we all love abilities that trigger when something enters the battlefield, don’t we? Well, Maralen, Fae Ascendant takes that to the tenth degree by bridging two of Lorwyn's most recognizable kindred types into a nimble value engine that’s entirely too fun to abuse. Whenever Maralen or another elf or faerie enters under your control, she exiles the top two cards of a target opponent's library, letting you cast one exiled spell each turn for free if its mana value is equal to or less than your Elf and Faerie count.

Verhey noted that "Maralen turned out awesome" and pointed out that "a lot of people have built that one." He has pitched team-up legends for years, and seeing her succeed makes him eager to explore more dual-type pairings like Rin and Seri or Olag and Miau.

It has been revealed that rather than singling out a single hero from the Turtle Power! Commander precon, the standout attraction here is the modular roster built around the “Partner — Character select” mechanic. Inspired by classic arcade beat-'em-ups, the keyword lets you mix and match eligible legends, like Leonardo, the Balance alongside Raphael, the Muscle or Donatello, the Brains, to tailor your Command Zone synergies.

As Verhey explained, "I think the interchangeable Character Select partner mechanic in the Commander deck is pretty awesome there." He added that he loves how these legends "can be interfaced and spliced together," noting that players have gravitated toward the pairings because they combine partner flexibility with punchy abilities. Pairing Leonardo, the Balance with Raphael, the Muscle gives you a prime example, since putting a +1/+1 counter across your board on token entry and doubling damage from creatures with counters lets modest boards turn lethal in a single turn.

In a recent development, at six generic, one black, and one green mana, Witherbloom, the Balancer carries affinity for creatures and extends that exact same cost reduction to every instant and sorcery spell you cast. Flooding the battlefield with tokens or cheap mana producers turns hefty spells like Army of the Damned and Shamanic Revelation into effortless plays. Once you pair that discount with token doublers like Chatterfang, Squirrel General, even splashy finishers like Exsanguinate or Torment of Hailfire become trivial to fire off for lethal.

According to recent reports, secrets of Strixhaven is loaded with what Verhey described as "banger commanders," and the designer admitted he could easily name around ten standout legends from the set. Even in that crowded lineup, Witherbloom, the Balancer rises to the top as a blast to build around, especially alongside spell-copying payoffs like Professor Onyx and graveyard recursion staples like Eternal Witness.

Sources indicate that this double-faced mythic rare gives Azorius builds strong flexibility at flash speed. On his front face, King T'Challa draws you a card whenever any player draws their second card each turn, and you can pay six mana total to transform him into Black Panther, Hope Enduring. The opposite side of the card yields a double-striking threat with flash that prevents damage dealt to him and draws cards on combat hits, making him especially lethal with equipment staples like Sword of Feast and Famine or unblockable auras like Steel of the Godhead.

Verhey pointed to T'Challa and Black Panther as a standout among cards that fit traditional color expectations while still "tearing up tables." Surrounding him with symmetric draw engines like Howling Mine or wheel effects ensures his front side triggers across every turn cycle before he flips to close out the game.

Industry observers note that at a single white mana, Nick Fury, Agent of S.H.I.E.L.D. looks modest on paper until you read his Power-up ability. Since Power-up reduces its activation cost by his mana cost when he enters that turn, Fury adds two +1/+1 counters to himself while digging seven cards deep to drop a Hero, Equipment, or Vehicle straight onto the battlefield. It’s solid flavor for a 2/1 creature, and has a lot of potential if you know the right way to abuse it.

Verhey described Fury as "really unassuming" yet potent, noting that "Nick Fury, the one-mana white commander, has been really strong." He also shared that he was running all five free spells once Fury hits the board for a single mana.

In a recent development, the Hobbit brought Middle-earth's more whimsical side to Commander with standout legends like Bilbo Baggins and Thorin Oakenshield, yet Smaug the Magnificent is an absolute beast among them. Built to snowball fast, the 4/3 legendary dragon with flying and haste, and even nets you a treasure token at the start of your upkeep. Worst of all, however, is Smaug’s main ability, which deals damage to any creature equal to the amount of treasures you have whenever he attacks.

Verhey noted that "Smaug Treasure decks look pretty cool" and called him a "really powerful Commander," which is saying something. For just four mana, the creature not only stacks treasures for you every single turn, but also deals a little extra damage where needed, best used to chip away at a player’s life total or creature-filled battlefield. Even worse is that Smaug can swing right when he gets onto the battlefield thanks to haste, so if you already have a slew of treasures by the late game, he’s dealing some serious damage that can be made even more devastating with red staples like Furnace of Rath and Fiery Emancipation.

It has been revealed that just like Smaug, Radagast of Rhosgobel also hails from The Hobbit set, bringing instant-speed tempo to mono-green decks. His static ability discounts the first creature spell you cast each turn by two generic mana and lets you cast it as though it had flash, essentially saving you mana for interaction before deploying threats on an opponent's turn.

According to recent reports, the Hobbit offers strong options across the board, according to Verhey, who mentioned, "I like the Radagast decks I've been seeing that discount your spells when you play one a turn." That opens the door for surprise plays like flashing in Kogla, the Titan Ape for instant removal or dropping discounted threats like Ghalta, Stampede Tyrant right before your untap step. While I’m not running him as a commander, I have a Radagast in my Thalia and the Gitrog Monster deck, which is all around sacking creatures and land.

As a color-shifted twist from the Reality Fracture Commander decks, Dack Fayden, Helping Hand, puts a fun spin on a well-known Magic character. Upon entering, Dack reveals cards from the top of your library until you hit creature cards equal to the number of your opponents. He then puts those creatures onto the battlefield permanently goaded and hands one to each opponent, stirring up chaotic table politics with a hint of group hug thrown in.

Sources indicate that calling the white Dack Fayden "kind of a funky one,” Verhey suggested he might be the answer for raw power in the set. Players who pair his trigger with blink staples like Ephemerate or symmetrical payoffs like Homeward Path and Trove of Temptation can quickly turn messy handouts into a one-sided advantage.

Recent findings suggest that liliana the Faultless flips familiar Magic lore in the Echoverse-themed Reality Fracture, becoming a white-aligned version of the character that gains you a life whenever another creature or planeswalker you control enters. You can also pay one mana and discard a card to grant another creature or planeswalker you control hexproof until the end of turn, giving mono-white decks a steady form of protection.

In a recent development, while Verhey also shouted out the set's white Leonin legends and his own black Abzan precon designs, Liliana fits neatly alongside those experiments. Her discard-to-protect clause pairs cleanly with planeswalker or token commanders like Elspeth, Sun's Champion and Mondrak, Glory Dominus that want extra shield equity.

True to his trickster reputation, Q, Stacking the Deck shuffles your library on entry and exiles cards from the top until he hits a nonland card, letting you repeatedly copy that exiled spell by discarding cards from your hand on your turn. Various brewers have already pushed this to remarkable extremes with 98-land decks built to guarantee hitting a specific combo piece.

Verhey admitted he still loves Q and wants "to believe that Q has something pretty wacky," framing him not necessarily as the strongest card in the set, but as one "on my radar" that plenty of players are already building around. Slotting Glaring Fleshraker into a 98-land Q deck, for example, demonstrates just how wild things can get, since exiling lands from your hand to chain copies of Fleshraker floods the board with Eldrazi Spawn tokens that pay for the next copy and ping the entire table out of the game in a single turn.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that “I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing.
  • Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews.
  • Recent findings suggest that the coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” said recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”.

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face.

Recent findings suggest that the coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”.

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the Fresh Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks noted “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”.

She noted, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal complications and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks mentioned “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”.

Sources indicate that one job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” noted Brooks.

“We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she mentioned. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”.

It has been revealed that since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”.

Sources indicate that “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

Recent findings suggest that she continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”.

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”.

Recent findings suggest that on the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” remarked Brooks.

Industry observers note that but regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that substantial machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”.

It has been revealed that “Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” stated Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”.

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting your gaming gear fix during the holiday shopping season is an annual tradition, but it’s more crucial this year than ever. The RAM shortage has driven up all electronics prices, right when the biggest game of all time arrives after a 13-year wait. So any discount you can score can have a major impact on your wallet. Before the main event starts, you can get started with some early Black Friday gaming deals here.

Sources indicate that game consoles are obviously more expensive than they used to be, even when they came out years ago. But bundle deals are still some of the best way to shave some cash off the sticker price. We’ve also got some deals on accessories, which aren’t always hit quite as hard by the component shortage, so there’s more room for savings.

In a recent development, well, let’s get the bad news out of the way up front: There probably won’t be that many deals on console hardware. Recent findings suggest that controlling your thermostat entirely from your iPhone or a HomeView can prove extremely convenient. That convenience can also save you money by making it easier to stay on top of your electricity usage.

Aqara’s W200 smart thermostat is a beautifully designed, easy-to-use accessory that comes with a bonus Apple feature that’s hard to find: Adaptive Temperature, which can remove lots of the need to manually update the thermostat.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re anything like me, you know the exact spiral that hits when your to-do list gets overwhelming.
  • That’s why I was equal parts skeptical and desperate when I slipped on the Neurable One — a pair of over-ear ANC headphones that pack 12 EEG sensors directly into the ear cushions to read your brainwave patterns in real time.
  • Normally $499, Neurable has knocked $50 off for Black Friday, dropping them to $449 through November 30 — and crucially, there’s no subscription paywall locked behind the app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re anything like me, you know the exact spiral that hits when your to-do list gets overwhelming. Your brain panics, you bounce between six smaller distractions to feel “productive,” and by 5 PM, you’ve somehow been busy all day while finishing absolutely nothing.

That’s why I was equal parts skeptical and desperate when I slipped on the Neurable One — a pair of over-ear ANC headphones that pack 12 EEG sensors directly into the ear cushions to read your brainwave patterns in real time.

Normally $499, Neurable has knocked $50 off for Black Friday, dropping them to $449 through November 30 — and crucially, there’s no subscription paywall locked behind the app. After testing them myself, I can confirm they genuinely work.

Save $50 on these brain-sensing ANC headphones that pack 12 dry EEG sensors into great-sounding 40mm beryllium drivers to track your focus, flag burnout before it hits, and keep you on task — with zero monthly subscription fees.

Sources indicate that first, let’s clear up the sci-fi paranoia: these aren’t reading your thoughts. The fabric sensors knitted into the memory foam pads pick up electrical patterns from your brain (no messy gel or electrodes required) and translate them into a live Focus Tracking feed and a Brain battery fuel gauge in the companion app.

Industry observers note that for a serial procrastinator (hi), having a live scoreboard for your attention is a game-changer. Starting a focus session turns staying on task into a literal workout for your brain: you can see the exact moment your concentration starts to drift, and the app nudges you to take Smart Brain Breaks before you hit the wall and doomscroll for an hour.

In a recent development, since I started working with these on, I’m noticeably getting more done in my day without feeling fried by the evening. But the weirdest, most welcome side effect? My sleep score actually improved too — likely because I’m finally respecting my mental bandwidth during work hours instead of trying to brute force through exhaustion.

Normally, some party trick comes at the cost of forgetting to make a good pair of headphones. Fortunately, Neurable’s first all-in-house design gets the audio fundamentals right.

The custom 40mm beryllium drivers sound crisp, balanced and genuinely enjoyable for long workdays — tuned for clean, fatigue-free listening rather than bloated showroom bass.

Yes, the companion app’s EQ options are limited, which is going to bug the hardcore audio tweakers out there. But to my trained ears, the out-the-box audio quality is strong enough that it’s nowhere near a dealbreaker.

You also get solid active noise cancellation, a clear latency-free ambient mode and Bluetooth multipoint for hopping between your laptop and phone.

Before you do buy, I’d be doing a disservice in not pointing out a couple of downsides with these cans:.

At $449, the Neurable one is still a serious investment — and if you just want the absolute lightest travel headphones with the greatest sound quality, there are plenty of mainstream options.

But if you struggle with distraction, burnout, or juggling ten half-finished tasks at once, these are the rare wellness wearable that actually earns its keep.

Getting a great sounding pair of ANC headphones and a personal focus coach for $50 off — with zero monthly fees — makes this one of the most interesting pair of cans I’ve tested this year, and my personal favorite Black Friday deal.

#154514. Industry News: ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

Industry News: ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.].
  • It has been revealed that “I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke stated in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale.
  • Sources indicate that lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.].

It has been revealed that “I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke stated in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”.

Sources indicate that lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter. Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

According to recent reports, he’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing new story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

Recent findings suggest that the finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

It has been revealed that “When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke noted. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”.

In a recent development, but Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

“I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo noted. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”.

Industry observers note that volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

“When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo mentioned. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”.

According to recent reports, “That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke stated. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”.

According to recent reports, in Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

Industry observers note that “This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke noted. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in New York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”.

“We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”.

“The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo said. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke stated. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”.

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”.

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other massive finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

Industry observers note that “The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo mentioned. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”.

Recent findings suggest that “And that’s what I did. It has this bit of nostalgia. It also has this magic to it and this dreamlike quality to what he’s doing,” Harjo mentioned. “The character is such an internal person that the only way you’re going to get those monologues is through a journal when he thinks it’s the privacy of himself and his journal. He’s expressing things that he wouldn’t normally express out loud.”.

“Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he mentioned, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

“Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke mentioned. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”.

Recent findings suggest that “But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”.

Industry observers note that one way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

In a recent development, “The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke stated. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”.

While another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo mentioned. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

Industry observers note that “The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke remarked. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”.

It has been revealed that how he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be announced is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple indicates the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

Industry observers note that the majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

Recent findings suggest that if your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Sources indicate that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. According to recent reports, plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

In a recent development, even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA indicates the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:.

In a recent development, if you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

It has been revealed that PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that amanda M. Castro is a Network TV writer at Collider and a Newly introduced York–based journalist whose work has appeared in Newsweek, where she is an Associate Editor, and The U.S. Sun, where she previously served as a Senior Consumer Reporter.

Industry observers note that she specializes in network television coverage, delivering sharp, thoughtful analysis of long-running procedural hits and ambitious new dramas across broadcast TV. At Collider, Amanda explores character arcs, storytelling trends, and the cultural impact of network series that keep audiences tuning in week after week.

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Amanda is bilingual and holds a degree in Communication, Film, and Media Studies from the University of New Haven.

In a recent development, few things are worse than meeting your intended partner's family for the first time. Add a remote mansion in the woods, a set of extremely questionable family traditions, and enough red flags to design a whole wedding reception, and elopement suddenly turns into a perfect idea. Rachel Harkin is in that exact situation when she meets her fiancé's relatives in Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen, an eight-part horror miniseries that turns wedding worries into something truly nightmarish.

In addition to being created by Haley Z. Boston, who has also worked on series like Brand Latest Cherry Flavor and Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities, it is executive produced by the Duffer Brothers – the creators of Stranger Things. Don't expect another monster-of-the-week show, though; this is a completely different form of horror. It's not based on being afraid of something that comes out of the woods to frighten you; instead, the horror comes from fears about family secrets, trauma from the past, and even the possibility that your loved one might not be the ideal person for you to be with forever.

Recent findings suggest that rachel (Camila Morrone) and her fiancé, Nicky Cunningham (Adam DiMarco), expect a relatively straightforward wedding week. They've traveled to the secluded Cunningham family home in the snowy woods of Upstate Latest York, where they'll exchange vows in an intimate ceremony surrounded by Nicky's relatives. One problem, however, is that Rachel has a terrible feeling about it all. Her instincts aren't exactly helped by the circumstances surrounding their journey. Strange encounters, disturbing discoveries, and increasingly ominous warnings make the trip feel like the opening act of an unfortunate true-crime documentary. Things don't improve when Rachel meets the Cunninghams; Nicky's family is wealthy, eccentric, and distinctly unwelcoming, with everyone seeming to know something she doesn't.

Recent findings suggest that the family features Nicky's mom, Victoria (played by Jennifer Jason Leigh), with a truly weird personality that seems hard to understand; Nicky's dad, Boris (Ted Levine), a doctor with a weird fascination for taxidermy; and Nicky's two brothers, Portia (Gus Birney), and Jules (Jeff Wilbusch). Portia's wife, Nell (Karla Crome), is also Nicky's former girlfriend. As Rachel spends more time with the family, their strange behavior becomes increasingly difficult to dismiss. Old stories, unsettling traditions, and mysterious warnings suggest something much bigger is happening. And with only five days until the wedding, Rachel has precious little time to figure out what's going on.

A horror story can only be as credible as the person the audience is following, and Morrone provides the series with a wonderful centerpiece performance. Rachel is observant, sarcastic, and much smarter than her companions realize early on. She certainly doesn't make the same mistakes everyone else does; she realizes something isn't quite right at the start. Unfortunately, knowing something is wrong isn't always the same as knowing how to escape it.

Recent findings suggest that morrone makes Rachel a compelling combination of vulnerability and stubbornness, so her increasingly desperate actions, even if difficult to witness, seem justified. There's also a lot of enjoyable personality beneath her worries, especially because she doesn't just respond as a victim of another Cunningham family issue. Meanwhile, DiMarco gives us an interesting contrast as Nicky, who looks very nice but is clueless about the severity of Rachel's fears. Their relationship has layers more complex than a simple horror-movie setup where a clueless guy is in a relationship with a suspicious girlfriend. The series also asks viewers what makes a relationship work, and whether loving someone is enough.

Leigh, Levine, Birney, and Wilbusch also make the Cunningham family an entertainingly unpredictable bunch. Birney deserves particular attention for her portrayal of Portia, whose enthusiasm and increasingly erratic behavior make her one of the show's more memorable characters.

The series' isolated setting works so well for a reason. The Cunningham estate feels like a place where visitors should probably keep their shoes on and their car keys close. Snow-covered landscapes, shadowy interiors, peculiar family portraits, and unsettling discoveries all contribute to the sense that Rachel has wandered somewhere she doesn't belong.

The directing team, led by Weronika Tofilska, does an excellent job establishing that unease. The cinematography, production design, and soundscape work together to make even relatively quiet scenes feel threatening. The show also knows when to lean into more traditional horror techniques, using jump scares and carefully constructed sequences to keep viewers guessing.

Industry observers note that the pacing requires some patience. The first part builds the mystery around Rachel and the Cunninghams before the full scope of the mythology emerges. The slower shift also lets the series move beyond the clichéd nightmare-in-laws narrative and explore other areas. In the second half, the storyline focuses primarily on Rachel and Nicky, exploring concerns like marriage, trust, and expectations in romance.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is at its most compelling when it brings those two sides together. There's plenty of gruesome horror, but the show's most uncomfortable questions are surprisingly recognizable. How well can you really know another person? What happens when the future you've planned suddenly feels wrong? And how much should you trust that little voice telling you to run?

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

It has been revealed that A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan). Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

Recent findings suggest that but that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Industry observers note that aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

According to recent reports, robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the big one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”.

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

The production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very swiftly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

It has been revealed that when you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

According to recent reports, but then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

According to recent reports, he’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

According to recent reports, just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone remarked to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

According to recent reports, and also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

Sources indicate that you are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

Recent findings suggest that I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a recent development, in a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”.

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”.

It has been revealed that they also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be vital one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”.

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

In a recent development, I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

According to recent reports, so, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they said my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

Sources indicate that I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

It has been revealed that I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s important to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and said, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

Industry observers note that the film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

Recent findings suggest that [Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

You are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

What do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

According to recent reports, I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

For more information about Tourette Syndrome and access to free resources and support, visit the Tourette Association of America right here.

Black Friday is finally here, and while you may have been on the lookout for a powerhouse PC before RAMageddon struck, sometimes it’s still worth checking out a more modest upgrade.

If your basic work laptop is barely clinging on, and it might be time to let it go to the big e-waste cloud in the sky, then the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i is well worth a look.

In fact, Amazon has dropped the price by a whopping 60%, bringing it from $869.99 all the way to $349.99 - a saving of over $500.

Save 60% on this laptop that we awarded 4 stars in our review, and even includes 1TB of OneDrive cloud storage and Microsoft 365.

At just 3.49lbs, the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i lives up to its name, but also manages to pack a sizeable 15.6-inch display that’s ideal for multitasking since you’re getting plenty of space for multiple windows.

There’s an Intel N100 CPU running the show, as well as an Intel UHD Graphics GPU. Look, it’s nothing to write home about, but for the tasks we mentioned earlier, you won’t need much more than that.

Sources indicate that plus, if you were thinking of paying out for Microsoft Office, there’s good news there, too: You get Microsoft 365 included in the box, as well as a whole terabyte of cloud-based OneDrive storage. That’s ideal for logging files, photos, videos, and anything else you want to store off your machine, and is very welcome since the 128GB SSD inside here is likely to fill up fast.

Industry observers note that in terms of connectivity, you’re getting two of the lesser-spotted USB-A port, as well as more modern USB-C, plus HDMI 1.4, an audio jack, and an SD card reader. If you’re planning to run some presentations through a large external display, this model has you covered.

In fact, the laptop has only one review so far, but it is a 5-star one, plus rapid charging means you can plug it in for 15 minutes and enjoy 2 hours of charge - ideal for getting work done in a pinch.

With Windows 11 preinstalled, this is a great way to modernize your existing laptop without breaking the bank - saving you a few extra pennies for other Black Friday deals, too.

Need more? Our reviewer said "it’s a great $799 laptop (if on sale)" (which this deal definitely is), on the way to awarding it a 4 out of 5 rating.
