[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”].

Sources indicate that A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next massive screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.” Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

Given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

It has been revealed that “All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino stated in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”.

Industry observers note that tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino stated that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report indicates that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting latest sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

According to recent reports, none of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character indicates that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

Sources indicate that when you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

Industry observers note that the film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the Fresh Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

Sources indicate that in a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

If you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the plans to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV indicates, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

The only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

Recent findings suggest that with AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

Industry observers note that with AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The firm says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

According to recent reports, I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the fresh speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 was not the one to rule them all on streaming.

The latest chapter of Prime Video's fantasy prequel series finds Middle-earth in its most dire state as Charlie Vickers' Sauron begins spreading his power throughout the world, all while Númenor is on the verge of civil war and Durin IV finds his rule over Khazad-dûm threatened by the return of his brother. Meanwhile, Rings of Power season 3 also followed Sauron's efforts to craft the One Ring to Rule Them All and build up his army of Ringwraiths.

It has been revealed that having premiered with its first four episodes on November 11, the Lord of the Rings series returned in grand fashion to Prime Video, securing its best reviews yet from critics and audiences alike with an 87% "Certified Fresh" score from the former on Rotten Tomatoes and 64% from the latter, breaking its streak of Rotten Popcornmeter scores. Prime also confirmed the premiere was off to a strong start for the season, bringing in 33 million viewers globally in its first two weeks, landing in the streamer's Top 10 of most-watched returning seasons.

Now, Nielsen has shared their own numbers from The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3's opening weekend, and it's a less flattering record for the show. Per the research firm, the four-episode debut scored 886 million minutes in the November 9-15 interval, landing the No. 1 position among original reveals, and No. 3 on the overall Top 10 chart, with the new episodes noted to have comprised "70% of watch-time" for the window.

Recent findings suggest that despite seemingly being a strong start for the season, it actually set a latest record-low for The Rings of Power, with the season 3 premiere being the first to come in below the 1 billion-minute-viewing mark. Season 1 memorably premiered with 1.25 billion minutes in its first four days, becoming Prime Video's first original series to top Nielsen's chart, while season 2 returned with a 1.02 billion-minute debut, similarly landing the top spot on the firm's Top 10 Originals chart for its premiere week.

In a recent development, it's certainly understandable that The Rings of Power has found itself continuing to trend downward with its Nielsen premiere numbers just in looking at audience reception to the Lord of the Rings prequel. Viewers have frequently taken to sharply criticizing the show online for its changes to J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, while more toxic people have targeted the show with racist hostility and labeling it as "woke." Moreover, the multi-year gap between Rings of Power's seasons clearly continues to be a hindrance in keeping viewers engaged with its returns.

Industry observers note that that being said, while the first Nielsen figures for The Rings of Power season 3 paint an unfortunate picture of its performance, the season as a whole is still largely outshining this negativity. In addition to the record-high Rotten Tomatoes scores, episode 7, featuring Sauron's epic forging of the One Ring, soared to claim the show's record for highest IMDb rating with an 8.5/10, beating the previous record-holder of 8.1/10, and the finale securing the No. 6 spot.

Recent findings suggest that with Prime Video already greenlighting The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power for season 4, which is expected to begin filming in Spring 2027, it's also clear the streamer is not discouraged by the slight decline as they push ahead with their five-season initiative. Given season 3's ending has starkly divided viewers over Sauron's bold decision, though, it will be interesting to see if this further impacts its Nielsen numbers in the future.

The entirety of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 is now streaming on Prime Video.

Set in the Second Age of Middle-earth, The Rings of Power explores the forging of the iconic rings, the rise of the Dark Lord Sauron, and the epic events leading up to the stories in J.R.R. Tolkien's classic novels.

In a recent development, reese Witherspoon can do it all, from breezing through law school in pink heels in Legally Blonde to alpha-momming her way down student halls in Major Little Lies. We can always depend on her for a gripping performance, and one of her most compelling roles is worth revisiting.

In Hulu's Little Fires Everywhere, Witherspoon once again steps into a Major Little Lies-esque maternal position in a wealthy community, but this time, she goes toe to toe with Kerry Washington. Both actors are magnetic on the screen together, creating a back-and-forth relationship that forces us to look at motherhood in a fresh light. All eight episodes are on Hulu, and watching these two get under each other's skin makes for a satisfyingly tense weekend binge.

Adapted from the novel of the same name by Celeste Ng, Little Fires Everywhere wastes no time throwing us into its central mystery of Elena's (Witherspoon) family house being set on fire. Cue the time jump to four months prior. Elena is exactly the kind of mother you would expect to find in the late-1990s, wealthy American suburb, Shaker Heights, one who meticulously curates her image and enriches her four high school kids' college applications with suitable extracurriculars. She also decides to rent out her family's rental property — at a charitable price — to a single mother and nomadic artist, Mia Warren (Washington), and her teenage daughter, Pearl (Lexi Underwood).

Sources indicate that A one-hit wonder is not a failure, it is a band that got one thing exactly right and never had to do it twice. Here is yours, what it claims about you, and the case for it being the best song on the list.

You are the one who starts it. This is a song that speeds up, slows down, changes key and ends somewhere nobody predicted, and it still gets an entire room on its feet in under four seconds, which is a decent description of how you operate.

You do not stay down. The entire song is one idea repeated until you believe it, which is exactly how resilience works in practice, and it is why it has soundtracked roughly every sporting comeback filmed since 1997.

Recent findings suggest that you feel it all and you want it on the record. This is a breakup song that stops halfway through to let the other person answer back, which almost no breakup song does, and it is why it sounds less like a complaint and more like a transcript.

Recent findings suggest that nobody can quite account for you, and you are fine with that. This is a fuzzed-out gospel rock song written by a Jewish folk singer who had been watching country gospel on television, and the fact that it works at all is the whole point.

Industry observers note that as the families become more intertwined through friendship and Elena's even more charitable offer of a job as a "house manager" to Mia, the tension between the two mothers steadily increases. Mia harbors a mysterious past and, as an investigative journalist, Elena can't quite let it go. When a custody battle over a baby girl also comes into play, the two mothers take opposite stances, which incites another exploration into their past traumas. Throughout the eight episodes, the conflict between them is riveting, especially as the show steadily unpacks motherhood with the nuances of class and racial differences.

As the title suggests, there are Little Fires Everywhere in this series, where each storyline ignites its own set of themes and tension, but the driving force of the show is motherhood. Much of it boils down to the complicated relationship between Elena and Mia, who are both drawn to and repulsed by each other's lifestyles, parenting behaviors, secrets, and identities. In the very first episode, there's an instance where Pearl and Elena's son, Moody (Gavin Lewis), aredriven home by neighborhood security due to trespassing. Elena scolds Moody, but very easily brushes the incident off, while Mia is rattled and reminds Pearl that the cops react differently to them. The show is quick to establish the differences between the mothers' circumstances, exacerbated by the later custody battle.

While Elena and Mia's approaches to parenting and their identities remain at the center, the custody battle further unravels layers of the show's discourse around the nuances of motherhood. It is a grueling case between Bebe Chow, who left her infant daughter at a fire station when she could no longer afford to feed her, and Linda McCullough, who has been raising the baby and hopes to adopt her. There is never a moment when we firmly believe one side should win, even as Elena and Mia make their stances obvious and crusade against each other. Little Fires Everywhere thrives in the gray area, never shying away from the bitter reality.

Sources indicate that though the rhetoric is heavy and harrowing, the way the show weaves its storytelling together allows us to be fully immersed. It ties the custody battle thoughtfully into Elena and Mia's rivalry and backstories, building on each other to paint this intricate portrait of motherhood. By also maintaining the rich and dynamic characterizations of these two opponents, the show anchors its wider commentary into our personal investment in their development. It's truly a captivating way to approach a timeless concept, one that you can easily lose yourself in during a weekend binge.

Recent findings suggest that with motherhood at the crux of the show, it is only natural that Witherspoon and Washington take the brunt of the responsibility of conveying its nuance. Similar to her role in Big Little Lies, Witherspoon hits the mark of the "perfect" suburban mother, but there's also an underlying desperation in Elena as she fights to control her black sheep daughter or walks on eggshells around Mia in fear of accidentally saying something offensive. Opposite her is Washington's erratic, suspicious, jaded, and equally desperate Mia, who balances parenting with her career and her trauma, never knowing where to draw the line. But together, they are arresting.

Witherspoon and Washington take to their roles beautifully, sustaining a chemistry and tension that is palpable whenever they are on-screen. Their micro-expressions clearly convey the attraction and discomfort Mia and Elena have at the beginning of the series, skirting the line artfully so we are hanging on their every twitch. As the relationship evolves into a more fearsome rivalry, their emotions feel primordial and vicious while maintaining an empathetic vulnerability that fleshes out the contentious nature of motherhood. We watch them make mistakes and struggle with impossible decisions, while still trying to cling to pieces of their identity outside of being a mother. It's a dizzying combination that sucks you right in.

These two are the powerful duo we never knew we needed to see on the screen together, so Little Fires Everywhere needs to be on your watchlist. As they bring their characters to life with moving performances, they flesh out the show's driving exploration of motherhood, one that never backs out from facing tiny details often left forgotten. With taut tension and emotion maintained throughout its eight episodes, the show makes for a gripping and gratifying experience, topped with two wildly overlooked performances.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:.

In the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season.

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

According to recent reports, no need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so swiftly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the big drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves quickly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other demonstrates tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

Recent findings suggest that the opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

It has been revealed that the latter goal is harder and, arguably, more notable. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) reveals up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

According to recent reports, there’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” issue, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

It has been revealed that outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

How Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of big, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

Industry observers note that so long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Industry observers note that either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover new sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

“The Hunting Wives” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 26 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something upcoming inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

It has been revealed that and by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

It has been revealed that “Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

According to recent reports, according to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”.

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

Recent findings suggest that “The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”.

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

According to recent reports, both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn mentioned. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”.

In a recent development, “What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”.

According to recent reports, one key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”.

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie stated yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”.

In a recent development, bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”.

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”.

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush noted.

“Hexed” is now playing in theaters.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ”The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” stands on its own as a beautifully written (by Quentin Tarantino) and directed (by David Fincher) Los Angeles noir that both invites and earns comparison with 1970s classics like “Night Moves” and “The Long Goodbye,” but its rewards increase exponentially the more familiar you are with its predecessor, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Although Fincher and Tarantino have both argued that the movie is less a sequel than simply another Cliff Booth adventure, the movie has quite a few fun Easter eggs to reward fans of Brad Pitt’s first time playing the laid-back stuntman.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

”The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” stands on its own as a beautifully written (by Quentin Tarantino) and directed (by David Fincher) Los Angeles noir that both invites and earns comparison with 1970s classics like “Night Moves” and “The Long Goodbye,” but its rewards increase exponentially the more familiar you are with its predecessor, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Although Fincher and Tarantino have both argued that the movie is less a sequel than simply another Cliff Booth adventure, the movie has quite a few fun Easter eggs to reward fans of Brad Pitt’s first time playing the laid-back stuntman.

It has been revealed that perhaps the most delightful callback to “Once Upon a Time” is the reappearance of two of cowboy actor Rick Dalton’s (Leonardo DiCaprio) collaborators on the “Lancer” pilot that took up a good section of the middle third of Tarantino’s earlier film. Co-star James Stacy (Timothy Olyphant) makes a brief appearance alongside “Lancer” director Sam Wanamaker, played once again by Nicholas Hammond, whose exuberant turn as the real-life actor-director in “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” was one of that film’s greatest pleasures. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

Hammond’s part is, like the other returning faces from “Once Upon a Time” (aside from Pitt, of course), essentially a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it cameo, but he was delighted to return to Tarantino’s world and to share the screen with Olyphant once again. He first heard rumblings that Wanamaker might return for “Cliff Booth” well over a year ago, when the assumption was that Tarantino would direct the script.

“Quentin has his team, and it’s the same crew that works on all his films,” Hammond told IndieWire. “I’d gotten to know them on ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,’ and a couple of the guys from the crew sent me emails saying, ‘Hey, it’s great we’re going to be working together again.’ Everyone had an ironclad NDA, so no one could tell me anything about the film, but that was my one little clue. Then, of course, when Quentin dropped out, and it looked like the movie was not happening, I thought, ‘There goes that chance.'”.

It has been revealed that hammond was elated, therefore, when Pitt resurrected the movie by giving the script to his friend Fincher. “Timothy and I knew that we were coming in basically as an Easter egg,” Hammond mentioned. “It was a tiny scene, and we knew that, but we were just thrilled that we were asked to come back, that Quentin thought it would be cool to have those characters back in the movie again. Let’s face it, he can get any actor he wants in the world to do anything, so it was an honor and a joy even though it’s a tiny little moment in the film.”.

In a recent development, when Hammond played Wanamaker in the first film, he saw an opportunity to pay tribute to all the talented, hardworking directors and actors who work in the industry without necessarily becoming A-list names — a category that includes himself. “Your career ebbs and flows,” Hammond said. “You do a lot of small roles on television or small roles in movies, and then you get your own series, or then you get a big movie, and that’s the life of most actors in Hollywood. Even people like Leonardo and Brad say they have tons of friends who were as good as them when they were all starting out, but so much of it depends on if the right role comes along at the right moment.”.

Recent findings suggest that hammond noted that for a lot of actors that moment never comes, but Tarantino has always recognized that that doesn’t make someone any less of an actor. “Most people think that if you’re good, you’re going to become a star. Quentin realizes there are a hell of a lot of very good actors out there who don’t become stars — that there are so many stars that have to align in the universe for that to happen. He admires and celebrates actors like Michael Madsen and Bruce Dern who have been journeyman actors their entire lives with moments of success, or flares of global recognition.”.

Industry observers note that hammond experienced one of those flares as a teenager, when he played one of the Von Trapp kids in Robert Wise’s classic musical “The Sound of Music,” and again several years later when he played Peter Parker on the CBS television series “The Amazing Spider-Man” — the role that made Tarantino a lifelong Hammond fan. “I’m fortunate in that way,” Hammond said. “I feel luckier than most actors in my situation, because I’ve had a few goalpost roles that the world is aware of.”.

Recent findings suggest that 60 years after he made it, Hammond still runs into “Sound of Music” fans all the time. “I was on a plane yesterday flying to Sydney, and a stewardess crouched down next to my seat and stated, ‘Nicholas, I just have to let you know that my family watches ‘Sound of Music’ every year,'” Hammond said. “‘When my grandmother was ready to pass away, she said the last thing she wanted was for all of us to gather around the TV together as a family and watch that movie.’ I don’t care how rich you are or how many movies you’ve been in, how many actors get a chance to be in a movie that has that kind of effect on people?”.

Industry observers note that hammond indicates that, having lived through the eras “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and “Cliff Booth” recreate, he knows Tarantino got that period of L.A. history completely right—something he attributes to the writer’s encyclopedic knowledge of his own work and that of all his peers. “There are very few people who could capture the 1970s as accurately as Quentin does,” Hammond said. “It’s his era. He grew up watching me as Peter Parker in ‘Spider-Man,’ and he watched all the episodes of ‘Gunsmoke’ I did, and all the episodes of ‘The Waltons’ and ‘The Brady Bunch.’ There’s not a show I was on that he didn’t see and know about.”.

In a recent development, in “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Hammond honored the directors of those episodic series whose names the public has forgotten, though Wanamaker, as an actor, was probably better known than many. When he got the part, Hammond was intent on playing Wanamaker with respect while still delivering on all the comic potential of Tarantino’s conception. “One of my fears when we were doing the film is I did not want Zoe Wanamaker to think we were making fun of her father, because we definitely weren’t,” Hammond said. “He was a very serious actor and a serious theater person.”.

Industry observers note that hammond took a deep dive into Wanamaker’s life and career for the part. “Quentin’s office sent me a stack of DVDs of movies that Wanamaker had directed, and movies that he had appeared in,” Hammond stated. “I got quite familiar with him. The Globe Theatre exists in England today solely because of him. If it weren’t for Sam Wanamaker petitioning and raising money and basically forcing the British government to authorize the building, the Globe wouldn’t be there. They wanted to build public housing there, and he managed to get a groundswell of support. And now, of course, it’s a huge tourist attraction, and in his honor the smaller studio theater within the building is called the Sam Wanamaker Theater.”.

Hammond claims he knew he was a part of something special when he saw “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” at its Cannes world premiere. “I’ve been lucky enough to be in three really significant films: [Peter Brook’s] ‘Lord of the Flies,’ ‘The Sound of Music,’ and ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,'” Hammond said. “With three very significant directors. So I’ve had a very fortunate career, and I still get excited just seeing my name on the call sheet. And when you’re working with people like Leo or Timothy Olyphant who are right at the top of their game, they’re the best of the best. I’m on the New York Yankees now, and when I get up to the plate, I better deliver.”.

Sources indicate that despite starring in several classics, Hammond is less interested in looking back than in whatever he’s working on now. “I absolutely love being an actor, and I love being on stage. I’ve done a great deal of stage work, and I’m always asked, ‘Which do you like better?’ And the answer always is, whatever I’m doing right then. When I walk into the stage door of a theater, I get exactly the same charge of excitement that I do walking onto a sound stage at a studio. I just feel like I’m home. I feel these are my people. These are the people that I’ve always been the happiest being with since I was 10 years old, and I that will never change.”.

Hammond looks to his “Sound of Music” costar Christopher Plummer, who did some of his best work late in life, as a role model. “I’ll do this as long as I possibly can. I’m of the Christopher Plummer philosophy that way,” Hammond mentioned. “The word retirement doesn’t really exist. What would I do? Give up the thing I love the most in the world to play golf? I’m not doing that.”.

Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

💡 Key Takeaways
  • WETA FX has been called upon to do visual effects for everything, from orc armies to superheroes, alien planetscapes to the innards of a whale.
  • Industry observers note that meeting that challenge often means the teams at WETA match and then build on live-action footage to get as close to a photorealistic look as possible.
  • Industry observers note that “Everybody was super stoked about this film because it’s so different from what we usually do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WETA FX has been called upon to do visual effects for everything, from orc armies to superheroes, alien planetscapes to the innards of a whale. On each project, they have to match the movie’s consistency. The goal is to make sure that the VFX blends perfectly into the overall visual style, not so unlike a certain Springfield dad creeping into a hedge.

Industry observers note that meeting that challenge often means the teams at WETA match and then build on live-action footage to get as close to a photorealistic look as possible. But adding digital effects to the wonderful world of stop-motion animation, as with “Wildwood,” WETA FX got to have more fun with creating a world that looks as textured and handmade as the puppets designed and animated by Laika Studios. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation.

Industry observers note that “Everybody was super stoked about this film because it’s so different from what we usually do. People got to be artists,” VFX supervisor Sabine Laimer told IndieWire. “We’re really good at making effects invisible, but here we could actually showcase the artistry. All of our people here loved it.”.

In a recent development, this applies to the way that WETA helped intensify battle sequences, the way they expanded sets so that they feel as fast as the impassible woods where most of “Wildwood” takes place, and the way they were able to match cinematographer Caleb Deschanel’s lighting to bring a unity to the digital and puppetry work within individual scenes. When designing the ivy that Alexandra (Carey Mulligan) seeks to control and that Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) seeks to pacify, WETA’s digital leaves weren’t meant to mimic real leaves in nature. They were built to look like the paper leaves a stop motion animator would use.

“[The leaves in ‘Wildwood’] have a different light transmission. They have a different level of detail, depending on how close the camera is to them,” Laimer mentioned. “[We developed] this sort of stage realism, if you want to call it that, rather than realism, and that makes a huge difference.”.

According to recent reports, one element where WETA needed to heighten the realism most was the ivy, which is eventually summoned into a sentient spire that threatens to overwhelm the entire world. “It’s alive, but it’s not a person. It has character, but it can’t feel like it’s a boss. It has to have intent, but it can’t be so direct that it feels like there’s a brain that’s going after the characters,” VFX supervisor Dan Macarin laid out the challenge of Laika’s brief to IndieWire.

“It had to creep, it had to attack, it had to consume, it had to overgrow,” Laimer added. “There was a lot of material there for us to work with, which was amazing, but we had to translate all of this intricate detail that they’ve built on their practical sets into a digital plinth environment and build it in a way that was malleable for us, and we had different stages of everything.”.

Sources indicate that laimer and her team tested ways to mimic the Laika animators’ practical work and drew inspiration from the natural world, like time-lapses of pea shoots with an uncanny, jerky motion as they grow. They built different vignettes that could be placed inside specific shots so the ivy would read as dangerous, but not distract from the drama between the characters. For the moments where the ivy threatens to overwhelm the entire plinth, the WETA team actually used fluid simulation to get the feel of the ivy being like a tsunami, this swelling of constant, growing motion that is headed in a definite direction, not just moving at random.

“We looked at practical references like schools of fish, where they move in unison and create shapes and change directions on purpose. It was a similar thing, or like flocks of starlings in the air. You have to sculpt the [ivy] cyclone per shot so that it’s not distracting in the background, it’s not too busy, but at the same time still feels like it’s alive,” Laimer remarked.

In a recent development, hitting that visual effects sweet spot was important in all the visual effects collaborations between WETA and Laika. The path to do that always ran through story, and what visuals would make the storytelling the most immediately legible to the audience. “WETA is really, really fantastic at doing third act battles,” Macarin stated. “We’ve done a tremendous number of them over the years and decades, and so it’s not the scope that we have to worry about. We can handle all of that. It’s always, ‘How do we tell this story?’”.

In the case of “Wildwood,” telling the story with visual effects meant simplifying a lot, so that even when we placed it behind the explosion of cannon fire (where it would never be safe for a practical camera to go), we still cared about the characters. “We were able to create aesthetic choices that still allow the audience to engage in the battle, but not necessarily put you suddenly into this photorealistic explosion or feel. This is a very colorful, emotionally driven sequence that just happens to have a battle around it,” Macarin remarked.

According to recent reports, the most fantastical-seeming choices in “Wildwood” are all about character. “They shot everything with two suns,” Laimer said. “They had a smaller, sharper key light and then a softer, wider one, which created this really beautiful falloff on the faces that we had to create digitally. That was really cool.”.

Industry observers note that getting to build expressive, beautiful worlds in animation — whether digital, stop-motion, or a combination of the two — usually is pretty cool, to be fair. And clearly, in the case of “Wildwood,” it brings out some of WETA’s best work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.

According to recent reports, upgrade 11/24: This upcoming setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Recent findings suggest that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”.

Google is now separating that preference into two upcoming options.

It has been revealed that this is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI customers on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:.

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”.

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, people, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”.

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is right now off, the two “latest settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying owners via email.

‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christopher Nolan‘s adaptation of Homer’s “The Odyssey” was one of the most awe-inspiring cinematic achievements of 2026, an epic worthy of comparison with the grandiose visions of David Lean and Stanley Kubrick.
  • According to recent reports, “We never really treated it in an epic way,” van Hoytema told IndieWire.
  • According to recent reports, given that, van Hoytema tried not to be seduced by the beauty of his surroundings if it didn’t serve the emotional experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christopher Nolan‘s adaptation of Homer’s “The Odyssey” was one of the most awe-inspiring cinematic achievements of 2026, an epic worthy of comparison with the grandiose visions of David Lean and Stanley Kubrick. Yet what interested cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema was less the story’s vast scale than the details of the human faces inhabiting the film‘s sweeping vistas.

According to recent reports, “We never really treated it in an epic way,” van Hoytema told IndieWire. “Even though we all know ‘The Odyssey‘ and understand the scale of the story, making some sort of a tourist film was never on our agenda. It was the characters and the visceral sense of their experience that we were interested in, so even standing in the most crazy places in the world — on mountaintops or wherever — we were never motivated by the landscapes. The settings take care of creating the scale and scope of the film — our perspective on the story was a very intimate one.” Related Stories Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face.

According to recent reports, given that, van Hoytema tried not to be seduced by the beauty of his surroundings if it didn’t serve the emotional experience. “It was less about showing how beautiful a beach was than about showing how shitty those men felt when they were on the beach,” he mentioned, noting that a key tool in getting across the characters’ internal feelings was shooting the film entirely in IMAX.

“Shooting an entire film in IMAX has been a pursuit of ours for quite a long time now, and we’ve been tweaking the lenses and tweaking the cameras in order to get there,” van Hoytema said. “We’ve managed to wrangle the equipment and technology around it to enable us to be right there next to you, looking straight into your eyes.”.

This again plays into that idea of intimacy versus scale, which was something van Hoytema and Nolan had experimented with in “Oppenheimer.” In that film, IMAX was used not only for major set pieces like the atomic bomb test, but quiet dialogue scenes shot largely in close-up. Van Hoytema claims that he and Nolan have long been aware that IMAX has historically been used mostly to depict the wonders of the world, but they wanted to expand its grammar.

Sources indicate that “The lenses that we use today are an evolution of different iterations of lenses that we have been building through the years, lenses that focus extremely close and that can open wide so that you can work with natural light or in half-darkness,” van Hoytema stated. “We’ve found that IMAX is an intimate format because it’s such a good replicator of the human experience and perspective.”.

According to recent reports, the biggest obstacle toward shooting an entire movie in IMAX before “The Odyssey” was always the sound — IMAX film cameras are famously noisy, making it difficult to get decent production recordings. “We built a blimp on ‘Tenet,’ but it didn’t work,” van Hoytema said. “This was the first film where we felt that the technology had gotten far enough to actually shoot the entire thing on IMAX. There’s been an evolution in development not only in my department but in the sound department — they have come up with better microphones, better filtration, and in this film it came together beautifully.”.

Industry observers note that van Hoytema and Nolan always had a backup proposal in case the IMAX cameras became too unwieldy or got in the way of performance, particularly in lengthy dialogue scenes that would outlast the cameras’ short magazines. Once Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway proved that they could pull off a complicated sequence in close collaboration with van Hoytema and the other departments, however, Nolan and his crew were confident they could rely on IMAX as their format of choice. “That day was the hardest, and we shot everything on IMAX, so for the rest of the film we just committed — no plan B,” van Hoytema said.

In a recent development, while van Hoytema and Nolan were enthusiastic about committing to IMAX, it did create massive logistical challenges — not just when it came to getting the heavy camera and blimp in and out of remote locations, but in terms of performance. The actors’ eyelines, for example, were often blocked by the enormous camera. “Here we are bragging about the intimacy we can achieve, and suddenly you’re on set with a gigantic black box in front of the actors, and they can’t look each other in the eyes,” van Hoytema said. “It was a huge problem.”.

To solve the problem, van Hoytema and his crew built a system that would allow the actors to see each other. “It was based on a teleprompter that has an angled mirror in front of the lens, and people can look straight into the lens reading a teleprompter because it has projected text on it. But instead of text, we had another mirror, and we had an actor sitting here. So basically what actors see is a little surface with a mirror with the other actor in there, and they can look straight into the other actor’s eye.”.

According to recent reports, van Hoytema could fine-tune the eyelines by adjusting the angles of the mirrors in what he called “a very analog but very effective solution. And the actors loved it, because instead of looking at a wall they’re literally looking at their co-stars.” Van Hoytema reiterated the idea that everything in the movie was geared toward character and performance — including, at times, making the actors as uncomfortable as possible.

“It’s not for nothing that Chris loves to go out at sea with a ship and do things that are almost physically impossible,” van Hoytema said. “The more miserable or real or wet the situation is, the more the actors have to react to and play with. And that also goes for my way of working. I love different weather situations. I love different light situations. I love kinetic and physical challenges. It adds something unexpected and something visceral. The camera’s always fighting something and the actors are fighting at that very same moment, so it becomes a weirdly symbiotic relationship to the elements.”.

In spite — or perhaps because — of the arduous shoot, van Hoytema didn’t want to see it end. “This was an extremely difficult film, but it was also the film where everything we’d been working toward came together,” van Hoytema. “We were much more light-footed. Weirdly enough, when what you’re doing becomes subjected to elements that you cannot control, you become a bit less precious. And that lack of preciousness is very liberating. We just went in headfirst.”.

If you’ve waited for the Black Friday sales to pick up one of the best carbon plate running shoes at a discount, your patience has been richly rewarded, because Puma has cut the price of the Fast-R 3 racer by 47%.

I test running shoes for a living and love testing racers in particular, and of the 50+ carbon plate super-shoes I’ve tried in recent years, the Puma Fast-R NItro Elite 3 is my favorite.

All colors of the Puma Fast-R 3 are reduced to $159 in the Puma sale, including my favorite 'Showtime' design with mismatched pink, blue and yellow shoes. It screams 'fast', which is fair because I think this is the speediest carbon shoe I've tested.

It’s my go-to option for race day, and I recently ran a 2:25 marathon in the shoe at the Frankfurt Marathon, having also run the London Marathon in it last year.

Like most super-shoes, the Puma Fast-R 3 pairs a springy midsole foam with a carbon plate, and has an ultralight design — it’s around 7oz in my US men’s size 9.5.

According to recent reports, where it sets itself apart from other racers is its plate, which you can see extends beyond the front of the shoe, and the aggressive rocker profile. These factors combine to create a highly efficient ride that helps you to keep rolling at race pace deep into your event.

Along with running two of my best marathons in the shoe I’ve also run my five-mile PR in the Fast-R 3, along with racking up well over 100 miles of training and racing in it.

All colors of the shoe are reduced to $159 in the Puma sale, and even though it’s excluded from the extra 20% off you can get on some Puma products with the code ‘CHEER’ right now, that’s a spectacular price for a shoe that normally sets you back $300.

Sources indicate that nick Harris-Fry is an experienced health and fitness journalist, writing professionally since 2012. He spent nine years working on the Coach magazine and website before moving to the fitness team at Tom’s Guide in 2024. Nick is a keen runner and also the founder of YouTube channel The Run Testers, which specialises in reviewing running shoes, watches, headphones and other gear.

Nick ran his first marathon in 2016 and became obsessed with the sport. He now has PBs of 2hr 25min for the marathon and 15min 30sec for 5K. Nick is also a qualified Run Leader in the UK.

Nick is an established expert in the fitness area and along with writing for many publications, including Live Science, Expert Reviews, Wareable, Coach and Get Sweat Go, he has been quoted on The Guardian and The Independent.

#154473. After 64 Years, DC Totally Reimagines Classic Villain

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (657 w)

After 64 Years, DC Totally Reimagines Classic Villain

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, many of DC Comics’ best villains were introduced during the Silver Age of Comics.
  • Industry observers note that just like what was done with Green Lantern, DC opted to have a upcoming character become The Flash rather than bring back the Golden Age version.
  • It has been revealed that wally has been on a dark path lately using his newly-discovered Flashes of Insight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, many of DC Comics’ best villains were introduced during the Silver Age of Comics. This was the era when Batman first battled heavy hitters like Mr. Freeze (originally named Mr. Zero) and Poison Ivy, while Superman found himself clashing with the likes of Bizarro, Brainiac, Metallo, and Parasite for the first time. However, The Flash was arguably the character who collected the most adversaries during the Silver Age.

Industry observers note that just like what was done with Green Lantern, DC opted to have a upcoming character become The Flash rather than bring back the Golden Age version. Barry Allen succeeded Jay Garrick in 1956’s Showcase #4, and he swiftly accumulated enemies like Captain Cold, Mirror Master, Gorilla Grodd, and Weather Wizard, most of whom also fight Wally West. Now one of the most powerful members of The Flash’s rogues gallery has been reimagined 64 years by going in a more heroic direction.

It has been revealed that wally has been on a dark path lately using his newly-discovered Flashes of Insight. The current Scarlet Speedster putting people in prison before they’ve even committed a crime based solely on these brief visions of the future was enough to raise the Justice League’s concern. Additionally, it was discovered that Wally’s overuse of the Speed Force was resulting in wormholes opening up in his pain receptors. Yet, Wally refused to stop looking into the future and taking the same courses of action.

Industry observers note that left with no other choice, Green Arrow and other Justice Leaguers battled with The Flash, believing that he's a danger to both himself and others. However, the combined might of Green Arrow, Wonder Woman, Aquaman, Jon Kent, Martian Manhunter, and the holographic Red Tornado wasn’t enough to get the job done. Enter Professor Ala Kazam, a woman whose name sounds a lot like Abra Kadabra, the aforementioned powerful Flash villain.

It has been revealed that ala Kazam appeared in the final pages of The Flash #39 to immobilize the present superheroes, reconstruct the arrow Wally destroyed that would have drained him of his speed, and then stuck him with the projectile. The only things this woman revealed about herself are that she’s from the future and that she came back in time to end “Flash’s reign of terror.”.

It has been revealed that as if the name and hailing from the future wasn’t enough to cement a connection to Abra Kadarba, Ala Kazam also appears to have the same powers as him. Abra, and presumably Ala, comes from the 64th century, where science and technology has become so advanced that it looks like magic to people in the present day. Ala is using the same kind of wand as Abra, and it contains enough power to instantly paralyze some of the most powerful Justice League members.

Industry observers note that however, it turns out Ala Kazam apparently isn’t the hero she claims to be. The cover for The Flash #41 demonstrates Ala suspending a Flash gorilla in midair, and the solicitation teases her as “a threat that knows more about them than they do themselves.” Then it’s stated in The Flash #42 solicitation that “all that stands between Ala Kazam and global destruction is a completely depowered Wally West,” and that it’ll take “the full effort of the Flash Family and then some” to defeat her.

What’s unclear is if Ala Kazam has sinister intentions like Abra Kadabra so often does, or if she truly believes she’s doing the right thing, but is working off of incorrect information and/or assumptions. It also remains to be seen if Abra himself will appear in this arc. Although the Absolute Universe’s version of Abra Kadabra was introduced a few months ago, the mainstream DC Universe’s Abra hasn’t been seen since roughly midway through Simon Spurrier’s run on The Flash.

The Flash #39 is now available from DC Comics.
