#154472. The 10 Greatest Rock Albums of the '60s, Ranked

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1324 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Collider ↗ Open Full Page

The 10 Greatest Rock Albums of the '60s, Ranked

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the '60s was a hugely important era for rock music – perhaps the most important decade for the progression of the genre.
  • The second album from chaotic British rock band Cream definitely made an impact.
  • Willy and The Poor Boys by Creedence Clearwater Revival is about as far as you can get from the psychedelic rock wave taking over the UK and the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the '60s was a hugely important era for rock music – perhaps the most important decade for the progression of the genre. Folk and protest influences were abundant, and the British Invasion was globalizing the genre. The counterculture was in full swing, bringing a psychedelic edge to rock and roll. The world was in a state of constant transformation, and the music of the decade mirrored this relentless change. Musicians began to experiment like they never had before, pushing the boundaries of what was possible – and what was socially acceptable. There was so much variety and innovation during this time that picking the top ten rock albums of the 1960s may seem like an impossible task. And, yet, here they are.

The second album from chaotic British rock band Cream definitely made an impact. An incredible amount of creativity and experimentation was packed into these eleven songs (clocking in at a mere 33 minutes.) Both of the singles released ahead of this album — “Strange Brew” and “Sunshine of Your Love” — charted in the UK, and the latter made it to number five in the US. Disraeli Gears bridged the gap between their earlier blues rock sound with the psychedelic tint they later took on. Perhaps “earlier” and “later” are the wrong words – the band dissolved after only three years together due to irreconcilable differences between bassist Jack Bruce and live-wire drummer Ginger Baker.

Willy and The Poor Boys by Creedence Clearwater Revival is about as far as you can get from the psychedelic rock wave taking over the UK and the US. This album is straight up Americana swamp-rock. The narrative storytelling and the focus on the American middle class make this album a stand-out and a fan favorite. The record was initially supposed to be a concept album, written and recorded from the perspective of fictional jug band Willy and The Poor Boys. While they didn’t end up following through with this idea, some of the texture remained – the story of the jug band that never was is expressed through the popular track “Down on the Corner.”.

Led Zeppelin II is widely considered to be the band's heaviest album. Their music style was evolving as the '60s slipped into the '70s – they were reshaping traditional American blues music into something with much more firepower. This album included three covers of Chicago-based blues songs and six original tracks. It was written while Led Zeppelin was on tour, recorded in myriad studios and cities (and even on Jimmy Page’s houseboat!) This constant relocation added to the chaotic feel of the album. But despite the constant motion, Zeppelin II comes together as a cohesive record, featuring dynamic shifts in volume and tone, driving guitar, and musical (rather than lyrical) hooks.

Electric Ladyland is the third and final album from the Jimi Hendrix Experience. The record initially confounded critics – they weren’t sure whether to love or hate the trippy, immersive, funky acid rock album Hendrix had created. It was an unprecedented piece of work, so some confusion is understandable. Nowadays, the record is regarded as one of the greatest albums in rock and roll. Hendrix referred to these songs as "sound paintings,” which is abundantly evident in the album. Each track is layered and ambient, drawing the listener deep into a bottomless well of sound. And lest we forget – this album also includes Hendrix’s legendary reinterpretation of Bob Dylan’s “All Along the Watchtower.”.

Jim Morrison and The Doors were a darker voice in the 1960s counterculture. On their self-titled debut album, the group mixes poetry, blues, psychedelia, and experimentation to create an incredibly important record. This record was developed through live performances, mostly at LA’s iconic venue Whiskey a Go Go. They released their single “Light My Fire” ahead of the album, which promptly got the public interested in their music. The Doors had an inconceivable impact on the bands that came after them, across a wide array of genres. Alternative rock and punk would not be what they are today without the music of The Doors.

Industry observers note that what's a rock and roll list without The Rolling Stones? Their eighth studio album Let It Bleed is a return to their earlier blues, gospel, and hard rock sound. The record was also heavily inspired by American roots music and the overwhelming feeling of disillusionment much of the Western world experienced throughout the 1960s. Let It Bleed includes some of their biggest hits to date, such as “Gimme Shelter” and “You Can’t Always Get What You Want.” Throughout the writing and recording of this album, the band was in a time of intense turmoil. Founding member and guitarist Brian Jones was slipping deeper into addiction and failing to show up for rehearsals, resulting in his termination from the group. He tragically passed away a few weeks later. He was replaced by Mick Taylor, and both musicians appear on the album. Keith Richards had to pick up a lot of the slack in the string section, which permanently altered the band’s sound. The release of Let It Bleed ushered in the band’s most successful period.

According to recent reports, tommy by The Who took six months to write and record — an unusually long period for bands at this time. This extended interval was well worth it, producing an iconic and unprecedented concept album. It would be impossible to rush the complex storytelling, theatricality, and groundbreaking scale of the record. Tommy, written by guitarist Pete Townshend, was the first album to be labeled a "rock opera". Townshend was inspired by Indian spiritual practices. The album follows the fictional Tommy Walker through his life, which is plagued by murder, abuse, and drugs. Tommy overcomes these myriad hardships to eventually become a messiah figure and spiritual leader. Tommy is widely considered to be The Who’s breakout album.

It has been revealed that highway 61 Revisited is Bob Dylan’s sixth studio album. In this body of work, we see Dylan depart further from folk music, incorporating an increasing number of rock musicians in the studio. This album is in many ways a continuation of his 1965 record Bringing It All Back Home. Dylan’s poetic lyrics capture the political and cultural unrest of America in the midst of the Vietnam War. His lyrics are steeped in clever allegory and impressionism, buoyed by a relentless blues-rock drive. With each album release, Dylan’s energy and rebellion grows.

Industry observers note that the Velvet Underground & Nico was greatly underappreciated during the time of its release. It is the band’s debut album, a collaboration with German model and singer Nico, a partnership that was carefully engineered by artist Andy Warhol. The record tackled unconventional and controversial subject matter like drugs and sadomasochism, which shocked the public — it was banned from many radio stations and record stores. The Velvet Underground’s avant-garde, abrasive sound did well in New York City’s underground scene, but pretty much nowhere else. They were well before their time, setting the stage for punk, alternative, and psychedelic rock. Many consider it to be the original art rock record. Today, it is finally appreciated for the masterpiece that it truly is.

Industry observers note that the Beatles’ Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band is a landmark psychedelic rock album – perhaps the most important body of work to come from the 1960s. This record was a huge moment in popular culture and helped to define the Summer of Love. It is an early example of a concept album, wildly innovative in every aspect of creation and production. The album is based upon a fictional band conceptualized by Paul McCartney and includes a vast array of whimsical and unusual influences, including vaudeville and circus music. This incredible album set the stage for prog rock and countless other genres, changing the face of rock and popular music forever.

Recent findings suggest that back in July, PrismML claimed its roughly 4 GB, 1-bit Bonsai 27B was the first AI model of its size to run on an iPhone. Now PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an update to the model it introduced in September.

The startup also drew attention when CEO Babak Hassibi told CNBC that Apple was evaluating its technology, as we reported at the time.

Sources indicate that the latest model is based on Qwen3.8 27B and keeps the same 5.9 GB footprint in its most compact format. This time, PrismML focused on helping the model handle longer tasks, including figuring out what to do when a tool returns an unexpected result or a step fails.

In a recent development, bonsai 2.5 improved on six of the seven benchmarks PrismML highlights. Its SWE-bench Verified coding score rose from 60.8 to 75.6, while its AppWorld tool-use score jumped from 51.2 to 90.5. LiveCodeBench v6 dipped from 83.8 to 83.0.

Recent findings suggest that what could that look like on a Mac? A coding assistant could inspect a private project, make a change, run the tests, and use the results to revise its fix. A document app could summarize a folder of sensitive files while keeping the processing on the device.

Industry observers note that prismML says Bonsai 2.5 runs on Mac, iPhone, and iPad through MLX. Its Apple silicon package is about 8.9 GB, and the model card walks through setup on a Mac. The weights are available for free under Apache 2.0.

For a closer look at how the model was compressed and tested, read PrismML’s technical white paper.

#154466. An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (486 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (486 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail.
  • I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail.
  • It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it ….

I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

It turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

Recent findings suggest that at the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the tech giant did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The latest rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

Sources indicate that so if you move a window to the corner of the latest machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The manufacturer solved this by a clever UI transition.

Sources indicate that what’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

You can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the company sweating the details.

#154465. 10 Best Movies That Unexpectedly Switch Main Characters, Including Psycho & Alien

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1677 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

10 Best Movies That Unexpectedly Switch Main Characters, Including Psycho & Alien

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some filmmakers deliberately lead audiences to believe they're following one character's story, only to shift the focus to someone else once the narrative is underway.
  • Of course, simply killing off a major character or changing perspectives doesn't automatically make for a brilliant twist.
  • It's a tricky narrative device to pull off, but these movies demonstrate just how much more memorable a story can become when audiences realize they've been following the wrong person.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some filmmakers deliberately lead audiences to believe they're following one character's story, only to shift the focus to someone else once the narrative is underway. Filmmakers have plenty of ways to play with expectations, whether by introducing an apparently obvious protagonist, giving a supporting character the kind of screen presence usually reserved for a leading role, or deliberately shifting the focus once viewers have settled into a familiar narrative. Done well, these tricks can completely transform a movie, turning an otherwise conventional story into something far more unpredictable.

Of course, simply killing off a major character or changing perspectives doesn't automatically make for a brilliant twist. The best examples establish a character who genuinely feels like the protagonist, giving audiences enough reason to invest in their journey before pulling the rug out from under them. Some are particularly effective because the replacement protagonist is even more interesting, while others use the change to explore an entirely different genre, theme, or perspective.

It's a tricky narrative device to pull off, but these movies demonstrate just how much more memorable a story can become when audiences realize they've been following the wrong person.

According to recent reports, quentin Tarantino's Death Proof is structured around two groups of women, with Kurt Russell's Stuntman Mike initially appearing to be the connecting figure between them. The first half gives audiences every reason to believe that Jungle Julia (Sydney Tamiia Poitier), Shanna (Jordan Ladd), and Arlene (Vanessa Ferlito) are the film's central characters – at least until Mike murders them.

It's an undeniably shocking change of direction, particularly because Tarantino has spent so long making the first group feel like the protagonists of a relatively relaxed hangout movie. The second half introduces Zoë (Zoë Bell), Kim (Tracie Thoms), and Abernathy (Rosario Dawson), whose confrontation with Mike turns the film into a very different kind of revenge thriller.

The switch is effective and shocking in its violence, but the first group aren't particularly developed, making them less compelling as some other pretend protagonists.

Barbarian makes excellent use of its changing perspectives, initially encouraging audiences to believe that Tess (Georgina Campbell) and Keith (Bill Skarsgård) will be the central pairing in a straightforward horror story. When Tess arrives at her rental property and discovers that Keith has already checked in, their uneasy relationship provides the foundation for the film's early tension.

Just as audiences begin to settle into that dynamic, Barbarian changes direction. A fresh section introduces AJ (Justin Long), a Hollywood actor whose arrival in Detroit initially seems completely disconnected from Tess's predicament.

Barbarian then gradually brings these separate perspectives together, revealing how their stories intersect in increasingly disturbing ways. This gives both sides of its narrative enough personality to make the change compelling. It's a terrific bait-and-switch, even if not the most sophisticated.

Few movies have as much fun misleading audiences about their protagonist as The Hunt. The satirical thriller begins by introducing a collection of strangers who find themselves being hunted by wealthy elites, but it repeatedly changes focus before settling on its actual central character.

Industry observers note that athena (Hilary Swank), Richard (Glenn Howerton), Randy (Ethan Suplee), Yoga Pants (Emma Roberts), Trucker (Justin Hartley), and Staten Island (Ike Barinholtz) all appear to have the potential to become the film's lead. However, nearly every apparent protagonist meets an abrupt and often ridiculous end.

Even Yoga Pants, whose star casting and extended screen time suggest she might finally be the person audiences should follow, is dispatched before the story reaches its real destination. Each character provides a different perspective on the political divisions and assumptions being satirized, setting up the narrative very effectively – though slightly hampering the audience’s connection with the real protagonist.

It has been revealed that stanley Kubrick's Full Metal Jacket doesn't quite pull off a conventional protagonist switch, but instead divides the story into two distinct halves. The first section focuses on Private Leonard "Gomer Pyle" Lawrence (Vincent D'Onofrio) and the brutal training regime imposed by Gunnery Sergeant Hartman (R. Lee Ermey).

It has been revealed that although Matthew Modine's Private Joker is present throughout, Pyle's increasingly tragic transformation appears to be the emotional core of the film. After the devastating conclusion of the training section, the story moves to Vietnam, where Joker takes center stage.

The change is striking, replacing the claustrophobic training camp with a very different examination of the Vietnam War. Through the two sections are connected by their exploration of military conditioning and the dehumanizing effects of violence, they have remarkably different characters, settings, and narrative priorities.

Wes Craven's Scream famously uses Drew Barrymore's star power to convince audiences that Casey Becker will be the film's central character. Barrymore was prominently featured in the marketing, and her presence gives the opening sequence the appearance of a traditional horror-movie introduction to its heroine.

According to recent reports, instead, Casey becomes Ghostface's first major victim, establishing that nobody is necessarily safe simply because they appear to be the biggest name in the cast. The decision is particularly clever because Scream is so knowledgeable about horror conventions.

Its characters regularly discuss the rules of slasher movies, including the tendency for audiences to assume that certain characters are protected by their apparent importance to the story. Craven uses that familiarity against viewers, making the opening murder a statement of intent for Scream's entire approach to genre expectations.

It has been revealed that the Place Beyond the Pines initially looks like a crime thriller centered on Ryan Gosling's Luke Glanton, a motorcycle stunt rider who turns to bank robbery after discovering he has a son. Gosling's star presence, along with the film's early focus on Luke's desperate attempts to provide for his family, makes him feel like the obvious lead.

Sources indicate that then Luke's story ends, and the film shifts its attention to Bradley Cooper's Avery Cross, the police officer involved in the events surrounding his death. It eventually moves forward again, following the sons of both men as they grow up and discover the consequences of their fathers' actions.

The three-part structure turns The Place Beyond The Pines's initial story about crime and police corruption into a multi-generational drama about inherited guilt, resentment, and the damage parents can pass on to their children.

Recent findings suggest that the Coen brothers' No Country for Old Men initially appears to be a straightforward chase thriller centered on Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin), a hunter who discovers a case of money at the scene of a drug deal gone wrong. His attempts to escape Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem) provide the narrative with much of its early momentum, and audiences naturally expect their eventual confrontation to determine the story's outcome.

However, No Country for Old Men gradually subverts this. Chigurh's relentless pursuit becomes more central, while Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) emerges as the film's moral and philosophical anchor. Moss's story ends abruptly, and No Country for Old Men refuses to provide the conventional showdown that viewers expected.

Instead, Bell's growing inability to understand or confront the violence around him becomes the real emotional focus. This change allowed No Country for Old Men to explore deeper themes than many Westerns, helping to modernize the genre.

Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather has one of cinema's most effective examples of an actor's presence misleading audiences. Marlon Brando's Don Vito Corleone dominates the film's marketing, its reputation, and its opening sequence. He's introduced as a powerful patriarch whose influence extends well beyond the criminal organization he commands, and his performance is so commanding that it's easy to assume he's the central character.

However, the real protagonist is his son Michael (Al Pacino), whose initial reluctance to become involved in the family business makes his gradual transformation all the more compelling.

In a recent development, it's a brilliant piece of character development, using an established crime boss as the origin story for an even more calculating successor. Brando's performance is so iconic that those who haven't seen the film can be surprised by just how much of it belongs to Pacino.

Ridley Scott's Alien initially gives audiences reason to believe that Captain Dallas (Tom Skerritt) will be its leading character. Skerritt was the most established star in the cast, and Dallas's position as commander of the Nostromo naturally makes him seem like the person who will guide the crew through their increasingly dangerous encounter with the alien.

It has been revealed that alien instead gradually shifts its attention towards Sigourney Weaver's Ellen Ripley, whose authority and practical instincts become vital. The transition is especially effective because Ripley isn't immediately presented as a conventional action heroine. She's a capable officer who follows procedure, challenges questionable decisions, and takes the threat seriously, even when her colleagues don't.

Recent findings suggest that once Dallas is gone, Ripley emerges as the most rational character and, by extension, is the person who audiences root for. This strengthens the film's feminist credentials, making it one of the most effective uses of the protagonist switch in cinematic history.

It has been revealed that alfred Hitchcock's Psycho is the definitive example of a film convincing audiences that they're following one protagonist before abruptly revealing that the story has entirely different priorities. Janet Leigh's Marion Crane is introduced as the central character, and the early scenes establish a compelling dilemma involving her dissatisfaction with her life, her decision to steal money, and her attempt to escape the consequences.

Hitchcock gives Marion enough depth and motivation to make audiences genuinely invested in what happens to her. Marion's murder is one of cinema's most famous shocks, not least because it happens before the film has even reached its halfway point.

In a recent development, hitchcock completely dismantles the narrative audiences thought they were watching. The stolen money, which initially seems central to the story, becomes largely forgotten, while the focus shifts to Norman Bates (Anthony Perkins), his unsettling relationship with his mother, and the mystery surrounding the Bates Motel. Countless movies have borrowed the idea, but Psycho remains the gold standard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a significant discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

According to recent reports, if you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink promptly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

Recent findings suggest that the X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing newly introduced firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

Forget The Lord of the Rings, These 4 Books Do Epic Fantasy Much Better

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that back in 1937, J.
  • Industry observers note that it's far and away one of the best epic fantasy books of all time, and for many years, it completely redefined and dominated the genre.
  • Canadian authors Steven Erikson and Ian Cameron Esslemont originally came up with the world of Malazan as a backdrop for role-playing games they made using a modified version of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons back in 1982.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that back in 1937, J. R. R. Tolkien published The Hobbit. This children's high fantasy novel about a home-loving hobbit going on a grand adventure rapidly became a critical and commercial success, and is still one of the bestselling books in history. That same year, Tolkien's publisher urged him to begin writing a sequel, and after several false starts, the story of the One Ring finally came to the author's mind. Over several years, what had begun as a concept for a relatively simple and straightforward sequel began transforming into something far bigger and more complex, bringing together worldbuilding and lore ideas from the rejected early drafts of The Silmarillion. Enter The Lord of the Rings, which was published in three volumes between 1954 and 1955. To this day, it's still generally remembered as the greatest and most foundational work of fantasy literature of the 20th century.

Industry observers note that it's far and away one of the best epic fantasy books of all time, and for many years, it completely redefined and dominated the genre. Going forward and well into the '90s, almost all high fantasy books published were in some way either inspired by or directly trying to imitate Tolkien. However, though it's undoubtedly one of the greatest works of speculative fiction in history, there are four particular books which arguably do epic fantasy even better. Sprawling worlds on a grand scale, large ensemble casts, deep lore that readers can't get enough of, and sky-high stakes are all characteristics of these undeniable masterpieces, which certainly give Lord of the Rings a run for its money. In the end, literary appreciation is entirely subjective, but there's a very strong argument to be made that these gems all understood epic fantasy even better than Tolkien.

Canadian authors Steven Erikson and Ian Cameron Esslemont originally came up with the world of Malazan as a backdrop for role-playing games they made using a modified version of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons back in 1982. The world and its lore eventually grew so large that the duo wrote a movie script titled Gardens of the Moon, but after that failed to find interest, Erikson and Esslemont agreed to each write a series set in Malazan. Erikson wrote the Gardens of the Moon novel, which was published in 1999 and thus kicked off the now-legendary Malazan Book of the Fallen, one of the greatest high fantasy book series of all time. Erikson agreed to a contract for nine sequels as soon as he sold Gardens of the Moon, and the result is a gargantuan fantasy epic composed of over 3.3 million words.

Indeed, the Malazan series was so large and so pop-culturally significant that once its final volume came out, it felt like one of those fantasy books that marked the end of an era. We are, of course, talking about The Crippled God, one of the greatest fantasy epics of the 2010s. Erikson, writing as an educated and trained archaeologist and anthropologist, took the genre blueprint built by Tolkien decades prior and crafted a conclusive chapter that's as exhilarating as they come. Larger in scope, more structurally complex, and more thematically mature than The Lord of the Rings, The Crippled God masterfully brings together dozens of storylines and hundreds of characters into a single chaotic collision. The resulting novel is as morally complex as it is philosophically profound, and that's why it's a must-read for any fan of the epic fantasy genre.

Sources indicate that the legendary Brandon Sanderson wrote throughout his undergraduate and graduate studies, with 12 novels already written by 2003 despite having no publisher or any offers of publication. It was in 2005 that Elantris, his debut novel, was finally published. Since then, Sanderson has become one of the most prolific speculative fiction writers of contemporary times, delivering several of the highest-rated books on Goodreads since 2000. Many of these books belong to his iconic Cosmere universe, composed of subseries as masterful as The Stormlight Archive. As exceptional as the series' first installment, The Way of Kings, was, it's the sequel that remains Sanderson's highest-rated book on Goodreads. It's Words of Radiance, the peak of 21st-century heroic high fantasy.

It doesn't feel quite as mythological as The Lord of the Rings, instead delivering a far more cinematic and character-driven experience that should appeal to anyone who tends to enjoy modern fantasy literature. For one, it's structurally perfect, a 1,000-page doorstop of a novel that nevertheless doesn't ever feel like it meanders. There's no fluff on the way to the Sanderlanche, a term fans have coined to describe the way Sanderson novels like Words of Radiance tend to culminate in fast-paced third acts where everything comes together in spectacular fashion to deliver a myriad of cathartic payoffs. Add to that a fascinating magic system, some of the most thematically layered and psychologically profound character writing that the genre has ever seen, and worldbuilding that even the most demanding epic fantasy readers should find satisfying, and you get a modern classic unlike any other. If there's any one fantasy novel that deserves to be called the best of the 21st century, it's this one.

Will George R. R. Martin ever finally finish writing A Song of Ice and Fire? Only time will tell. But even if the long-awaited The Winds of Winter never came, one thing would still remain undeniably true: A Storm of Swords is the last fantasy epic masterpiece of the 20th century. Back in the '90s, Martin had been wanting to take a stab at epic fantasy writing since reading the works of Tolkien, eventually coming up with the idea for A Song of Ice and Fire, now widely regarded as one of the greatest and most influential fantasy book series of modern times. It helped prove that the genre was more than ready to tell stories far darker, more mature, and more morally complex than what Tolkienesque high fantasy had been delivering for decades. The third book in the series is A Storm of Swords, still remembered by many as not only the best chapter in A Song of Ice and Fire so far, but also as one of the best fantasy novels ever written.

In a recent development, it is, at the very least, one of the best fantasy books since 2000; a bleak, exciting, brilliantly paced masterpiece that went on to win the 2001 Locus Award, be nominated for the Nebula Award for Best Novel, and become the first novel in the series to be nominated for the Hugo Award. There's no denying that there could never have been any Song of Ice and Fire—nor, by proxy, Storm of Swords—without Tolkien's influence in Martin's writing, but that's exactly what makes this novel so exceptional. Crafted in many ways as a direct subversion of many a Tolkienesque epic fantasy trope, A Storm of Swords is as politically complex as it is emotionally devastating. Balancing death, tragedy, action, and psychological realism to utter perfection, Martin delivered one of the most brilliant works of dark fantasy in history, culminating in an entire second half that's as breathtaking and propulsive as The Lord of the Rings' best battles.

It's complicated to compare ancient tales and myths to modern fantasy, since both genres are so dramatically different yet so essentially intertwined. Nonetheless, no one would call anybody crazy for saying that Homer's Odyssey does epic fantasy better than not only The Lord of the Rings, but practically any other epic fantasy book ever written. It is, after all, the fantasy epic par excellence, the poem that laid down the foundational blueprint for how Western writing would approach the fantasy and adventure genres forevermore. It established the core tropes of the genre long before "fantasy" actually existed as a properly distinct literary category, and is still a must-read for pretty much anybody and everybody with the ability to read a book.

Born as an oral tradition and not put into writing until around the mid-6th century BC, The Odyssey is the literal bedrock on which the entire Western epic literary tradition is built, which almost makes it unfair to compare any other subsequent masterpiece to it. Indeed, there aren't very many fantasy epics better than The Lord of the Rings, but if there's one whose superiority is pretty much undisputed, it's Homer's masterpiece. That's because, far from only being historically crucial, The Odyssey is so timeless that it's arguably still just as entertaining as any other epic fantasy masterwork. Intelligent, full of high-stakes set pieces, and infinitely analyzable from start to finish, it's the most perfect work of epic fantasy the world has ever seen.

Without further ado, let's dive into the best Netflix thriller movies to watch this week.

There wasn't a bigger horror movie this year than "Obsession. Written and directed by Curry Barker, the psychological horror-thriller grossed nearly $525 million against a reported budget of under $1 million and made stars out of its leads, Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette, the latter of whom is getting Best Actress buzz for her unsettling performance.

If you haven't checked out "Obsession" yet, the freaky flick centers on Baron "Bear" Bailey (Johnston), a hopeless romantic harboring a serious crush on his work friend Nikki Freeman (Navarrette). However, when he makes a desperate wish on a mysterious "One Wish Willow" novelty toy that Nikki would reciprocate his feelings, it causes the young woman to spiral into a frightening and violent obsession.

Watch "Obsession" on Netflix now.

Sources indicate that written and directed by Marie Kreutzer ("Corsage," "The Ground Beneath My Feet"), this slow-burn psychological thriller stars Léa Seydoux as Lucy Weiss, a successful concert pianist who moves from Munich to the German countryside for a fresh start with her husband, Philip (Laurence Rupp), and their young son. However, when the police turn up at their door early one morning with a devastating accusation against her husband, Lucy must confront how little she knows about her spouse.

At the same time, police investigator Elsa Kühn (Jella Haase) not only has to navigate the Weiss family's case but also her own father's cognitive decline and troubling allegations against him.

Watch "Gentle Monster" on Netflix now.

There are few settings more pulse-quickening than a battlefield, a fact that director and co-writer Peter Berg taps into for this post-Pearl Harbor war thriller.

Based on the 2022 Buzz Bissinger non-fiction novel "The Mosquito Bowl: A Game of Life and Death in World War II," the story follows four American college football players—played by Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson, and Tom Francis—who enlist in the Marine Corps and, to momentarily forget about the brutal horrors of being on the front lines, participate in a Christmas Eve football match ahead of the Battle of Okinawa.

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he states can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

Sources indicate that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having remarked that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a upcoming paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having remarked that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing tech giant with millions of users.

Sources indicate that ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

Industry observers note that “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and remarked, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

In a recent development, over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing newly introduced here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and remarked, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

Sources indicate that the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one tech giant or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that revealed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from significant data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

Recent findings suggest that when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand upcoming model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For significant data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very promptly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Recent findings suggest that could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Upcoming tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an vital piece of the puzzle.

Industry observers note that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

It has been revealed that ng: In AI, data cleaning is key, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

Industry observers note that for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

In a recent development, ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

Sources indicate that “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Recent findings suggest that synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

It has been revealed that to make these complications more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and notes it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

According to recent reports, how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

According to recent reports, ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift problem. I find it really key to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

It has been revealed that ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s notable for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with iPads running the same chips as Macs, many have wished Apple would give us the option of running macOS on them instead of the somewhat clunky iPadOS windowing system. Apple’s previous arguments against converging devices have been somewhat weakened by the launch of the touchscreen MacBook Pro.

A upcoming report claims that Apple already has iPads running macOS internally, and that work on a giant iPad continues, but don’t hold your breath for a public launch of either ….

As iPad hardware has grown more powerful over the years, the software has struggled to keep up. We saw split-screen capabilities first, with full windowing finally coming to the devices in iPadOS 26 last year.

The UI is still rather clunky compared to macOS, however, leading a significant number of people to wish that Apple simply offered the option of using the more powerful operating system on its tablet devices.

I would be comfortable with 11" and 13" devices running macOS. Actually, I don’t require them to run macOS itself, but I do need them to run macOS apps. I wish the iPad could match a MacBook’s productivity. Running macOS on an iPad seems like a reasonable idea. The MacBook Air is now the better price choice, while those needing a powerhouse will always choose a MacBook Pro or Studio.

Some suggest that running macOS on iPad would reduce Mac sales, but I disagree. I own a nearly full-spec MacBook Pro 16" and expect to keep a machine like that, yet I also purchased a MacBook Air for lighter travel. I would prefer an iPad over the Air, but I cannot choose it because it lacks the apps I require. If it supported them, I would buy the iPad Pro with all accessories, and Apple would gain more revenue from me. I appreciate the concept of owning an iPad, but presently it lacks the value needed to justify paying more for a device that simply does less than a MacBook Air.

In a podcast Q&A, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman notes that Apple is already doing this internally, but there’s no sign of any plans to make it available outside the organization.

Sources indicate that apple has iPads internally running macOS, and they’ve had that for some time. The fact that they have the underlying architecture of Apple Silicon that’s the same on the iPad and the Mac gives them the flexibility in order to test these types of things.

In terms if they’re actually going to do it – would they bring macOS to the iPad itself – at this point I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon. I’ve checked into this and there’s no ongoing operating system project right now in terms of a brand fresh operating system for the iPad – there is no work being done to consumerize macOs on the iPad.

Gurman notes Apple seems set to continue to make piecemeal changes over time to bring iPad capabilities closer to those of the Mac but is showing no signs of full convergence.

He reiterated that work on a long-rumored giant-sized folding iPad continues.

Recent findings suggest that the other thing I want to say is that I’m really excited for this potential of Project J312. That is, this giant 19-inch, 20-inch foldable iPad. And it’s basically like a gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside.

However, he notes there’s no guarantee it will ever launch, saying the timings have already slipped from 2027 through 2028 to 2029, but both cost and yield challenges may still kill the project. If it does launch, it’s expected to cost anywhere from $3,000 to $5,000.

#154447. Newly introduced York and California age gating rules go into effect in the new year

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1411 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eff ↗ Open Full Page

Newly introduced York and California age gating rules go into effect in the new year

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eff

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different.
  • According to recent reports, EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts.
  • Sources indicate that three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for Fresh York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

According to recent reports, EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on consumers.

Sources indicate that three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.

Along the same lines as the California regulations, Newly introduced York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

According to recent reports, as we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the Fresh York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

Industry observers note that the New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in Fresh York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

Industry observers note that when young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current concerns. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.

Sources indicate that at the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Substantial Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.

Sources indicate that legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, Upcoming York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org.

Industry observers note that take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.

Industry observers note that if these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet people meaningful choice and control.

Batman: Arkham Asylum was every bit as atmospheric as some of the character’s darkest comic book adventures, and its combat system would go on to influence an entire generation of action games. More impressive still was Rocksteady's ability to build upon that success with two exceptional sequels.

The 2011 release of Batman: Arkham City earned a staggering 96 on Metacritic for its PS3 version, while Batman: Arkham Knight brought Rocksteady’s trilogy to a close in 2015. More than a decade later, all three games can be purchased together for considerably less than the price of a single movie ticket.

According to recent reports, the Batman: Arkham Collection is officially 90% off as part of PlayStation’s Black Friday sale, bringing its price down from $59.99 to just $5.99 through Monday, November 30. The digital PS4 collection is also playable on PS5 via backwards compatibility and includes the remastered editions of Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, alongside Arkham Knight and their previously released downloadable content.

Sources indicate that in addition to the three main campaigns, the collection includes several adventures that give members of the extended Bat-Family their own time in the spotlight. Among them is Arkham Knight’s A Matter of Family, which follows Barbara Gordon as Batgirl prior to the events of Arkham Asylum, and Harley Quinn’s Revenge, an additional story set after the events of Arkham City. The collection also includes several alternate costumes inspired by Batman’s cinematic history, allowing players to patrol Gotham in Michael Keaton’s 1989 Batsuit or even take the Batmobile from the classic Adam West television series out onto the streets in Arkham Knight. However, 2013’s Batman: Arkham Origins, the prequel developed by WB Games Montréal that explores an earlier encounter between Batman and the Joker, is excluded.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Rocksteady’s influence on Batman’s gaming adventures extends to this year’s LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight. The TT Games release incorporates several familiar elements from the Arkham trilogy into its open-world Gotham City, including its approach to combat and stealth. Rocksteady is even credited as a co-developer on the project, with approximately two dozen of the studio’s developers contributing to the game.

Batman: Arkham Collection is available for $5.99 on the PlayStation Store through November 30.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card.
  • In a recent development, as of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place.
  • The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV.

In a recent development, as of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc.

The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own.

Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc….

These new forks generally all have a few things in common:.

… and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model, on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate.

In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster.

Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last.

That said, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy.

Enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts. It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds.

If you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published.

podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1.

This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server:.

My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the important lines.

I imagine upgrading would be pulling a newly introduced image down, though I have not tried this yet.

On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L) with MTP enabled:.

Strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next.

Industry observers note that * It’s worth noting that between these two groups, vllm-radiance made an appearance, which was a fork of vLLM with AMD-specific patches. I tried this too, but the build steps were so onerous and vLLM so overbuilt for my specific use case (1 machine, 1 developer), that I abandoned it and went back to vanilla llama.cpp.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone 17 was arguably one of the biggest upgrades Apple gave its base iPhone in years. And even though the iPhone 18 Pro series is now here, I still think the iPhone 17 is the phone most people should buy if they're looking to get an iPhone this year.

Thanks to a Black Friday iPhone 17 deal at Metro by T-Mobile, you can now get one for just $729, saving you $200 without trading in your old phone.

The iPhone 17 may be over a year old at this point, but there's still a lot to like about this phone. One of the biggest upgrades Apple introduced with this generation was the 6.3-inch OLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. Apple had previously reserved 120Hz refresh rates for its Pro models, but bringing it to the standard iPhone 17 gave consumers one less reason to spend extra on a Pro model.

And while the A19 chipset is no longer Apple's latest, it's still more than capable of handling pretty much anything you'd want to do on your iPhone. Moreover, unlike the previous base model iPhones, you also get 256GB base storage with the iPhone 17, so you don't necessarily need to spend extra on a higher storage variant.

In our iPhone 17 review, we described the phone as offering "better upgrades than the Pros." The phone also lasted 12 hours and 47 minutes in our battery life test, which should be enough to get most people through a day of regular use.

There is one thing worth keeping in mind with the Metro deal, though. The iPhone will remain locked to the carrier for at least 365 days after activation, meaning you won't be able to use another carrier's SIM or eSIM during that period. Get the unlocked 256GB iPhone 17 directly from Apple for $929 and receive a $75 Apple Gift Card through November 30. Select "Connect on your own later" to avoid committing to a specific carrier.
